Product Culture

Bunai Factory Systems: The Friday Walk-Through

A case for discussion; it does not resolve.

1. Coimbatore, Sunday 4 October 2026, 10:50 p.m.

The north-east monsoon had arrived early, and from her terrace in R.S. Puram, Revathi Balan could hear water in the storm drain below. On the cane table were the agenda for the leadership offsite that began at nine next morning on Avinashi Road, a laptop open to a spreadsheet Sneha Mahadevan had sent from Toronto at 6:14 p.m., and a WhatsApp message from Arvind Rajagopalan, founder and chief executive of Bunai Factory Systems. It read, in full: "Revathi, keep tomorrow simple. One question only. Are we going to trust our people or our process? Both is not an answer."

Revathi had been Chief Product Officer for eleven months. The board met on Friday 9 October to approve the FY27 product plan and a second tranche of the hiring freeze. On 20 October she was due in Dubai for Bustan Retail Group's quarterly review, whose contracted dates, on the current burn-down, Bunai would miss by a quarter. Between those dates she was expected to say what Bunai's product organisation actually was, twenty months after the company spent ₹11 crore and most of its senior engineering goodwill on becoming a different kind of product company.

She had drafted four options. She did not believe any of them was the question.

2. How Bunai got here

Bunai was founded in Coimbatore in 2015 by Arvind Rajagopalan, a third-generation textile man who ran his family's spinning unit for nine years before deciding the industry's real bottleneck was not machinery but paper. Its first product replaced the handwritten line-production register with a shop-floor tablet: by Friday a factory manager in Tiruppur knew which of his sixty lines had lost an hour and why. It sold the way such things sell in the Tamil Nadu clusters — Arvind drove to the mill, walked the floor, and left with a purchase order on a letterhead.

By FY26 Bunai was a manufacturing-execution and buyer-compliance platform serving 312 plants across 118 customer groups — Tiruppur knitwear exporters, Karur home-textile mills, garment units around Bengaluru and Gurugram — on ARR of ₹84 crore. A ₹190 crore Series B in November 2021 had funded a Pune engineering centre, a three-person Berlin design studio near the European buyers, and a New Jersey sales office under Jerome Fernandes. Of 470 staff, 214 sat in product, design, data and engineering.

Two earlier decisions shaped what Revathi could now do. The first was the Bustan contract of August 2023: ₹28 crore over four years to deploy Bunai across 74 supplier plants feeding Bustan Retail Group's Gulf and East African stores, with eleven sub-modules, a schedule fixed in an annexure, liquidated damages of ₹1.2 crore per quarter capped at ₹4.8 crore, and a termination right after two consecutive misses. The board minuted it as a beachhead: a Gulf logo and a compliance module resellable to every buyer-facing exporter in India.

The second was Project Karigari, approved in January 2025 after Bunai lost a nine-plant deal to Hiranya Plant Intelligence, a better-funded Bengaluru rival whose deck had one slide Bunai could not answer: outcomes, not orders. Karigari put 214 people into eleven squads, each with a product manager, a designer, a data partner and quarterly outcome targets instead of feature lists, and installed an evidence gate: nothing entered a build queue without eight logged customer conversations, a baseline number and a metric to move. Arvind championed it publicly and, Revathi had come to see, never believed it.

Exhibit 1 — from board minutes, the Karigari charter and the release log. Dates of belief, not discovery.

3. The industry

Indian apparel and home-textile exporters live inside other people's deadlines. A Tiruppur knitwear unit shipping to European and Gulf retailers is judged on on-time-in-full delivery, on audits against buyer codes of conduct, and increasingly on traceability paperwork driven by European due-diligence law. The domestic side of the same factory serves Indian brands and marketplaces — Reliance Retail, Flipkart, Meesho, Nykaa's fashion business — with shorter cycles and different data demands. GST e-invoicing pulled financial documentation into software; the DPDP Act has pulled worker data, biometric attendance included, into a consent regime most plants have not implemented.

Competition came from three directions. Global ERP suites, implemented by Infosys or TCS, owned the enterprise layer but sat far from the floor. Hiranya priced aggressively and sold an analytics story to chief executives. Below, Zoho's low-cost applications and a tail of Excel-and-VBA vendors kept Tiruppur's pricing expectations low. Jio's coverage had made shop-floor tablets viable in Karur and Erode; it had also made every mill owner's nephew a potential competitor.

The exposure was asymmetric. Domestic plants were 71% of ARR and churned slowly; export and Gulf accounts were 29%, grew fastest and carried the contractual teeth. Revathi's organisation was funded by the first group and governed, in practice, by the second.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The first two quarters looked like vindication. Anja Krüger's Berlin studio ran Bunai's first true discovery programme, 140 interviews in nine months; the gate rejected eleven proposals in Q1 FY26, two already floated to prospects. Arvind read the numbers out at the 2025 Deepavali all-hands. Three things believed then are no longer safe to believe.

The first was that the evidence gate would raise adoption. It did, on the measure Bunai chose (Exhibit 2). But by Q2 FY27 Sneha's analysis suggested a selection effect nobody had designed for: small, well-scoped problems cleared the gate in days, while structurally important ones needed three weeks of floor immersion the gate's interview count did not recognise as evidence. The gate did not reward evidence. It rewarded provable smallness.

The second was that the Bustan module would be reusable. Three of eleven sub-modules had been adopted by any other customer; Bustan's audit taxonomy, Arabic-first interface and Ramadan and Eid calendars had turned the beachhead into a bespoke build consuming, by Ketaki Deshpande's reckoning, a fifth to a third of capacity — the range itself a finding, since contract work sat under one epic (Exhibit 5).

The third was that empowerment was a structure. Through FY26 senior engineering attrition ran at 31%, against 12% in FY24, as Bengaluru and Chennai firms hired Bunai's staff engineers at 40–55% above the Coimbatore band. Empowered squads need people senior enough to be trusted with judgement; the judgement left, the process stayed. By mid-2026 squad decisions were quietly being re-made in Arvind's Friday walk-through, an informal review he had run since 2016, where he reported what he had seen on that week's factory visit and reset priorities. Twice in FY26 he was right when the data was not: he killed a piece-rate dashboard validated with eight interviews, saying no supervisor would expose it to a union representative, and insisted on the Karur packaging module that now carries ₹7.9 crore.

Then, in February 2026, Nikhil Barve's Squad 7 went around the gate. Hansraj Knitwear Exports, a 6,000-machine Tiruppur group and Bunai's second-largest domestic account, had given notice of non-renewal. Nikhil moved himself and two engineers borrowed from the Bustan queue into the plant for three weeks, and shipped a line-balancing and work-in-progress tool in seven weeks with no logged interview and no baseline metric. Hansraj renewed for three years at ₹6.4 crore, and the tool now appears in 38 of the last 52 new-business conversations. Nikhil had done more customer discovery than any squad in the company and had violated the discovery process to do it. The leadership team could not agree which sentence mattered.

5. The people

Arvind Rajagopalan, Founder and CEO, Coimbatore. Position: the company drifted into ritual and must return to the mill floor. Incentive: a Series C conversation in FY28, where the Gulf logo matters more than process maturity. Not saying: that he now regards Karigari as his own mistake, and that the walk-through is the only place he still feels like the man who built the company.

Ketaki Deshpande, VP Engineering, Pune. Position: the binding constraint is capacity, not culture, and the annexure has eaten it. Incentive: her centre is measured on the burn-down, and a missed milestone lands on her. Not saying: that her own tracking is too unreliable to prove it, and that two of her best engineers want to move to Squad 7.

Jerome Fernandes, SVP Global Sales, New Jersey. Position: the gate cost two Gulf deals and must not apply to committed accounts. Incentive: FY27 quota weighted 60% to export logos, paid on bookings, not retention. Not saying: that his team fills the CRM's "reason won" field from memory, making Exhibit 3 a record of what his sellers believe.

Anja Krüger, Principal Designer, Berlin. Position: the gate was never the culture; the culture is who may decide, and here that is one man on a Friday. Incentive: her studio's charter rests on discovery staying a gate, not a service. Not saying: that four of the eleven Q1 FY26 rejections were, privately, for being inconvenient to the Bustan schedule.

Sneha Mahadevan, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: every number in the pack is weaker than the confidence with which it is quoted. Incentive: she gains from saying so, but a 10.5-hour offset means she says it in writing, after decisions are made. Not saying: that the celebrated adoption metric was chosen because instrumentation could already produce it.

Cheryl Tan, Director of Customer Success, APAC and Gulf, Singapore. Position: the domestic base, which pays for everything, has had no roadmap of its own for six quarters. Incentive: her renewals are domestic, her escalations Bustan. Not saying: that she quietly routes customers' requests through Nikhil, because that route works.

Nikhil Barve, Group Product Manager, Squad 7, Coimbatore and Tiruppur. Position: judge squads on outcomes and get out of the way. Incentive: he is the current hero and knows the story has a shelf life. Not saying: that the build left ₹2.1 crore of debt in the scheduling service, that he took Ketaki's engineers without telling her for eleven days, and that he doubts it generalises past a floor he grew up beside.

Ayesha Hameed, Group Head of Sourcing, Bustan Retail Group, Dubai. Position: the annexure is the annexure; her board approved a supplier-visibility programme on those dates. Incentive: credibility on a programme she sponsored. Not saying: that only 46 of 74 plants have finished master-data cleanup, giving her reason to want a renegotiation she cannot propose.

6. Exhibits

Revathi had cut a nineteen-page pack to the exhibits she expected to be argued about. Exhibit 2 was Anja's, Exhibit 3 Jerome's; different systems, and they disagreed.

Exhibit 2 — Features released FY26–Q2 FY27, by gate status

The contract row holds nine sub-modules only Bustan may use: denominator all accounts, addressable base 74 plants. Clients below build 41 are partly uninstrumented; 8–11% of sessions go unlogged.

Read naively, Exhibit 2 says the gate works and Exhibit 3 says it does not. Together they say something less comfortable: the gate produced many small adopted things and few things anyone bought Bunai for, while the releases that bypassed it were slower, stickier at nine months and disproportionately present in won deals — on a sample of six, credited by those who sold them. Exhibits 4 and 5 are no steadier: a pulse rating autonomy 4.1 of 5 sits beside exit interviews from a different seniority saying the opposite, and 17% of capacity arrived unlabelled.

Exhibit 6 was the slide Jerome liked and Cheryl dreaded. A 142% retention on three accounts, one of whose growth is written into an annexure, is not a market signal; it is a contract. The 104 domestic plants that pay two-thirds of the bills returned 103%, against a roadmap none had been consulted on since 2024.

Exhibit 7 — from the Karigari charter (solid) and from sprint records, the annexure and interviews (dashed). The published operating model is the top row only.

7. Voices

From the offsite pre-read thread, 2–4 October.

"Twenty-two gate-cleared releases, ₹4.6 crore. Nineteen deals on one tool built by three people who ignored the process. I am not against research, only against paying twice for it."

— Jerome Fernandes, New Jersey, 2 October, 11:07 p.m.

"Jerome is quoting a field his own team fills from memory, a third of it blank. If we are to run this company on Exhibit 3, let us ask a customer first."

— Sneha Mahadevan, Toronto, 3 October, 8:40 a.m.

"Nikhil did not skip discovery. He did it properly and skipped our paperwork. That the two came apart is the finding. We built a gate a form can clear and three weeks on a shop floor cannot."

— Anja Krüger, Berlin, 3 October, 1:22 p.m.

"Then the other obvious thing. Whatever we decide about gates, 27% of my engineers are on eleven modules for one Dubai customer, three of which have ever been sold elsewhere. I can give the squads autonomy or Ayesha her annexure. Someone above me must choose."

— Ketaki Deshpande, Pune, 3 October, 6:05 p.m.

"Twenty-two years in this trade and I never learnt anything important from a survey. I learnt the packaging module from a supervisor in Karur redrawing our screen on cardboard. Tomorrow, do not bring me a framework."

— Arvind Rajagopalan, Coimbatore, 4 October, 4:18 p.m.

"Our board approved visibility across 74 plants on the annexure schedule. I understand you have organisational changes underway. I cannot present organisational changes to my board."

— Ayesha Hameed, Bustan Retail Group, Dubai, 1 October, e-mail

8. The options as Revathi sees them

A. Re-assert the gate, with no exceptions

Treat Squad 7 as a breach, restore Karigari in full, make the walk-through an input rather than an override. Defends the ₹11 crore spent and the stated values; also asks the company's most effective product manager to accept publicly that the way he saved ₹6.4 crore was wrong, and leaves the gate's bias to small work untouched.

B. Two speeds, made official

Ring-fence a contract-delivery group against the annexure; let the rest run on outcomes. Honest about Exhibit 5, protects the ₹4.8 crore exposure. But it is close to what exists informally already, and creates a permanent second class doing bespoke work at Coimbatore bands while the outcome squads get the interesting problems — the gradient attrition runs down.

C. Generalise Squad 7

Dissolve the gate, fund four immersion squads on the Squad 7 model, judge them on outcomes alone. Rests on the evidence Revathi trusts least (Exhibit 3), needs seniority the company is losing at 31% a year, and assumes an approach built on Nikhil's lifelong access to one Tiruppur family travels to Karur, the NCR units and Dubai.

D. Change who is in the room

Leave the process alone and change the forum: replace the walk-through with a fortnightly review where squads present outcome movement, Cheryl brings two domestic customers live onto the call, and anyone overriding must say what evidence would change their mind. Cheapest to try, hardest to make real, and it needs Arvind bound by something he founded the company to avoid.

She had written all four, then added a fifth line and left it unfinished: "All four are about process. Every artifact here is about authority — who may decide, and what counts as knowing." She was not sure that was insight rather than an elegant way to avoid Monday.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Bunai held ₹61 crore of cash against a burn of ₹4.2 crore a month — fourteen months — and the board had frozen hiring but for two DPDP-related security roles. The annexure carried ₹1.2 crore per quarter of liquidated damages capped at ₹4.8 crore and a termination right after two consecutive misses; the next milestone fell on 31 December 2026, inside the post-Deepavali shipping peak, with Deepavali on 8 November closing most plants for four to six days and freezing deployments a fortnight either side. The DPDP consent rework was not optional and took 9% of capacity. Senior engineers in Coimbatore had to be offered ₹28–34 lakh against ₹46–58 lakh in Bengaluru, and she had no approved headcount at either number. She had eleven squads, no new people, a contract she could not rewrite alone, and a board told in January 2025 that this was solved.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did Project Karigari actually change at Bunai, and what did it leave as it was? Use Exhibits 4, 5 and 7, not the charter.
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 point opposite ways. What must be true for each to be the reliable one, and what evidence obtainable before Friday would most change your reading?
  3. Was Squad 7's Hansraj work a failure of Bunai's product culture, an expression of it, or a symptom of something else? What does that imply for how Nikhil is treated on Monday?
  4. Arvind's walk-through has been right and wrong. When is a founder's proximity better evidence than a squad's instrumented research, and how would an organisation tell the difference in advance rather than hindsight?
  5. If Revathi's unfinished fifth line is right — that the live question is authority and what counts as knowing — what does a defensible plan look like against the annexure, the freeze and the December milestone?
  6. It is 9 a.m. on Monday 5 October. What does Revathi do first, and what does she tell the board on Friday about a transformation it approved twenty months ago and has twice been told is working?

At 11:35 p.m. the rain stopped. Revathi deleted the four option slides, restored them, and read Arvind's message again. Both is not an answer. She was fairly sure that was the one thing in the pack that was straightforwardly untrue, and she had eight hours to decide whether saying so on Monday morning would be leadership or the end of her tenure.

People, Leadership & Organisation · Product Organisation & Management · Exp40

Product Culture, Measured

Evidence over opinion, outcomes over output, customers in the room — and the arithmetic that decides when each of those three is wrong.

1. Two decisions that look like process and are not

On 5 February 2026, Kaushik Ramanathan, Chief Product Officer of Brihat Ledger Systems, reached the third agenda item of a Pune board meeting and realised he was losing an argument he had not prepared for. Brihat sells reconciliation and treasury software to forty-one Indian banks and NBFCs; FY26 recurring revenue was ₹310 crore, built by sixty-two engineers in nine squads. The slide on screen came from his own product operations lead. Brihat had shipped forty-eight features in FY26 on 1,056 engineer-weeks: at a loaded ₹48,000 each, ₹5.07 crore of capacity. Eleven could be tied, twelve months on, to a named customer outcome: a renewal saved, a module upsold, a support line that fell. Thirty-seven could not.

A board member, formerly CFO of a listed NBFC, proposed the obvious remedy: nothing ships without five documented design-partner interviews and a problem statement signed by the account team. Kaushik was to return on 14 April with a plan. He believed, without being able to prove it, that the remedy was worth less than nothing in his particular business — and that saying so would sound exactly like a product leader defending sloppiness.

Six days later in Bengaluru, Farida Qureshi, Vice President of Product at Bhramari Speech Cloud, faced the mirror image. Bhramari runs voice agents handling 3.1 million calls a month for fourteen lenders. Under review was a Hindi-English code-mixed collections agent promised to a large NBFC's board for 22 April. Bhramari's evaluation suite — 1,840 utterances scored against a rubric — returned 91.2%, its best ever. Then a staff engineer, unprompted, hand-graded 300 live pilot calls: 78% were acceptable. The suite was 6% code-mixed; live traffic in the pilot districts was 41%.

Both look procedural; both are cultural in the sense developed below. Each turns on what counts as proof before money is spent, what counts as a result, whose voice reaches the room, and who pays for carrying an inconvenient number.

2. The idea, and the five camps that disagree about it

Define product culture operationally: the distribution of behaviour an organisation exhibits under low supervision. Four behaviours carry the weight: what evidence is demanded before engineering time is committed, what counts as success and is rewarded, who is admitted to the room where commitments are made, and what happens to someone whose bet fails.

The lineage runs through disciplines that never merged. Edgar Schein (1985) separated artefacts, espoused values and basic assumptions, and observed that only the third predicts behaviour — which is why values pages are poor instruments. Deming held quality to be a property of the system, so punishing individuals for systemic defects suppresses the information needed to fix them. Amy Edmondson's 1999 work inverted the intuition about safety: higher-performing hospital teams reported more errors, because reporting was safe. Ron Westrum's 2004 typology — pathological, bureaucratic, generative — was the first culture construct with a survey instrument attached, carried later into DORA and Accelerate (2018). The product tradition is younger: Amazon's working-backwards memo, Spotify's 2012 squads paper (disavowed by its own author), Perri's build trap, Cagan's Empowered, Torres's continuous discovery. Under all of it sits Christensen's resources-processes-values framework, in which values are the prioritisation criteria a cost structure sets.

Table 1 — Five schools, as propositions each would sign and refuse.
SchoolWill signWill not sign
Team design (Cagan, SVPG)A feature team cannot be exhorted into evidence-driven behaviour; change what it owns and behaviour follows.That artefacts and cadence alone move anything durable.
Information flow (Westrum, Edmondson, DORA)How an organisation handles bad news is the highest-leverage variable, and it is measurable.That empowerment is the mechanism; safety and flow sit upstream of it.
Founder standards (the Bezos and Jobs lineage; the 2024 “founder mode” argument)Taste propagates from named individuals and decays when delegated into process.That the team closest to the customer holds final say on quality.
Operations (product ops)Culture as stated is unfalsifiable; change artefacts, cadence and instrumentation and behaviour follows.That beliefs must change first.
Economic determinism (Christensen RPV)Evidence standards are downstream of gross margin and the cost of failure.That a culture programme moves an organisation whose economics punish patience.

The last row is omitted from most training material and is most often right. Brihat's 78% gross margin buys patience; a quick-commerce operator at 4% contribution margin cannot fund a six-week discovery loop, and calling that a cultural failing is a category error.

3. Mechanics: five load-bearing parts, and the arithmetic under one of them

Experts do not work on culture in general. They work on five mechanisms, each with an observable inspectable in an afternoon and changeable by a named person.

Table 2 — The five mechanics and their readings at both companies, February 2026.
MechanicObservableBrihatBhramari
Evidence thresholdWhat the amount of required proof is a function ofNone; proof discretionary, estimate mandatoryEval pass rate above 90%, applied uniformly
Decision rightsWho may say no, and what it costs themAccount team may veto; squad may notNobody had standing to hold a launch on a sample
Outcome algebraWhether team metrics can all rise while the company metric does notSquads own delivery, not outcomesPods own a proxy, not an outcome
Failure protocolThe 72 hours after a bad launch, and the next promotion cycleTwo FY26 rollbacks; both owners kept their squadsUntested
Contact dosageHours per PM per month, and whether the sample matches the served populationHigh dosage, four loudest accounts out of forty-oneNear zero; contact mediated by the eval suite

The first mechanic has a formal treatment, and it makes Kaushik's instinct rigorous. Treat a discovery gate as a diagnostic test applied to a population of candidate features. Brihat's FY26 population was forty-eight: thirty-seven duds, eleven not. Average build cost was 22 engineer-weeks, or ₹10.56 lakh. Finance attributed ₹26 crore of retained and expanded ARR to the eleven — ₹2.36 crore each. Five interviews plus a prototype cost ₹1.4 lakh of loaded time, so gating all forty-eight costs ₹67.2 lakh a year.

Now the error rates. On Brihat's retrospective sample a discovery pass correctly flagged two-thirds of eventual duds: sensitivity 0.67, saving 0.67 × 37 × ₹10.56 lakh = ₹2.62 crore. Against that sit false kills — some fraction f of the eleven good features abandoned because five interviewees did not want what their institution would later pay for. Net value is ₹2.62 crore − ₹0.67 crore − f × 11 × ₹2.36 crore, or ₹1.95 crore − ₹25.96 crore × f.

Break-even is 1.95 ÷ 25.96 = 7.5%. A gate that wrongly kills one good feature in thirteen has erased its entire saving. That is the content of Kaushik's instinct, and it generalises: where payoffs are fat-tailed, uniform evidence gates are frequently negative-value, and the expert response is to make the threshold a function of the cost of being wrong rather than the cost of building.

Two second-order effects follow. Any threshold in units the team controls is gamed at the notch: when Brihat piloted a gate at fourteen engineer-weeks, scoped estimates grew a spike at twelve and thirteen and a hole at fifteen — the bunching economists see below tax thresholds. And gates shift work toward what is cheap to test: a ₹4 crore treasury-limits redesign is hard to prototype, a dashboard filter validates in a day.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

The doctrine — evidence over opinion, outcomes over output, customers in the room — rests on four conditions, each testable, each failing somewhere.

One: the cost of being wrong exceeds the cost of finding out. For Bhramari this passes overwhelmingly — hand-grading 300 calls costs ₹40,000 of analyst time against an agent carrying exposure under the Reserve Bank of India's fair-practices expectations on recovery communication. For Brihat it passes at the median and fails in the tail.

Two: outcomes are attributable to a team inside a horizon shorter than the planning cycle. Bhramari passes in hours. Brihat fails: an enterprise renewal resolves in twelve months, so ownership there must run on leading indicators — thirty-day activation, tickets per thousand transactions — or become an annual verdict nobody can steer by.

Three: the organisation survives being told bad news. The diagnostic is not a survey but the last rollback. Brihat passes on two FY26 rollbacks whose owners kept their squads. Bhramari's protocol was untested, and the route the 300-call sample travelled — off the books, via someone with no standing to stop anything — suggests the answer was unknown.

Four: the evidence is representative of the population served. Bhramari fails on 6% against 41%. Brihat fails differently: four accounts that answer the phone, out of forty-one that pay.

Three situations make the doctrine misleading rather than merely inapplicable. In safety-critical and licensed domains, shipping to learn is prohibited, and a culture prizing fast feedback produces shortcuts around controls. In zero-to-one markets there is no extant user to consult, and demanding evidence yields the incremental version of what exists. In design-led products whose value is coherence, aggregating preference regresses to the mean; the disciplined form of evidence is craft judgement held by named people.

5. Hard edge cases, and what happens at the seams

Multi-product companies do not have a culture; they have a weighted average. Variance between two squads in one building routinely exceeds variance between two companies, because the proximate cause of behaviour is the director two levels up. A programme measured at company level shows a placid mean concealing a bimodal distribution, and the failing half stays invisible until it loses a customer.

Two-sided businesses meet attribution in its sharpest form, since one side's gain can be paid out of the other's surplus and both movements are real. Regulated products carry a second evidence system that does not talk to the first: compliance sign-off is evidence about legality, not value. Hardware-plus-software runs on two clocks. At Banjaara Field Devices, which makes handheld inspection units for utilities, firmware is gated by a fourteen-week tooling cycle while the companion app ships weekly, so “test before you commit” means a laboratory pilot to one group and a 2% traffic flag to the other.

AI-native products change the evidence organ itself. When behaviour is non-deterministic, the unit of evidence becomes a graded evaluation set: a sampled population, with every sampling problem that implies. Bhramari's 6%-against-41% gap is the canonical failure: an eval suite is a survey instrument, and an unrepresentative survey yields confident, precise, wrong numbers. Once a pod is measured on pass rate, the eval becomes the product.

The seams are where mature organisations least resemble their published descriptions. A platform team has no external customer, so the remedy is to name an internal one and measure adoption — which works until adoption is mandated, at which point the metric measures the mandate. What large companies actually do, and rarely say, is run two cultures: a gated core where changes are expensive to reverse, and an ungated edge where they are cheap. Those who manage it badly keep one published standard, honoured in the core and ignored at the edge.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert from the competent

The promotion packet is the culture document. Tell: read the last five promotion cases and count how many were argued on shipped scope. The obvious reading — that values statements set culture — is wrong because those are cheap signals and a promotion is an expensive one. Rewriting the values page before the rubric changes nothing, and advertises that fact.

Gate on reversibility, not size. Tell: whether the evidence rule references engineer-weeks. A pricing change touching every contract is three engineer-days and nearly impossible to unwind; a redesigned reporting module is four hundred engineer-hours and revertible in an afternoon. Size-based thresholds feel fair and are dimensionally wrong.

Psychological safety is about the cost of speaking, not pleasantness. Tell: whether the most junior person in a review ever contradicts the most senior, and whether the meeting then proceeds normally. The reading that safe teams are harmonious inverts Edmondson's finding that safe teams surface more problems. A team with no reported defects is exceptional or silent; the base rate favours silent.

Blameless does not mean accountability-free. Tell: whether post-incident actions have a named owner, a date, and someone who checks. Safety without standards produces a comfortable organisation that learns nothing; standards without safety produces an anxious one that hides.

Customer presence degrades into customer theatre. Tell: whether any clip played in a review has ever contradicted the slide that followed. Dosage without the authority to change the agenda is decoration.

Local metrics must sum honestly. Tell: add up what every team claims and compare it to the company number. If the sum exceeds the whole, teams are trading a shared resource — subsidy, traffic, a shared surface — and calling the transfer an outcome. This reads as a measurement problem; it is a design problem, fixed by a centrally owned ledger of shared constraints.

Rituals decay into their form, and the dead field marks it. Tell: a template field nobody has filled for three months, still present in every document. Its persistence means the artefact is produced rather than used. People fill in what is read, so the dead field locates exactly where reading stopped.

Evidence standards are partly bought, not chosen. Tell: gross margin and cash cycle. A 78%-margin vendor can absorb six weeks of discovery; a 4%-contribution operator cannot, and importing the first one's practices into the second imports a cost structure the business does not have. The obvious reading calls this an excuse; the expert reading calls it a constraint to design within, which means cheaper evidence rather than less.

7. Where product type and stage genuinely change the answer

Table 3 — What differs across product types: the instrument, and how it fails.
TypeDominant evidence formCharacteristic failure
ConsumerExperiments at volume; cheap and fastSignificant local wins that never aggregate into retention
B2B and enterpriseDesign partners, win-loss, telemetry from few accountsThe loudest account's roadmap mistaken for the market's
Platform and marketplaceTwo-sided instrumentation; incrementality testsOne side's gain booked as a company outcome
Hardware plus softwarePilots, field returns, long-cycle validationTwo clocks, two vocabularies, mutual contempt at the seam
AI-nativeEvaluation suites plus live samplingEval becomes the product; suite drifts from traffic

Stage changes the causal route rather than the destination. At thirty people, culture is the founders' habits, propagated by proximity and correctable in a conversation. Between roughly one hundred and five hundred it becomes whatever the director layer measures and promotes on, and this is where most degradation occurs, invisibly, in rubrics nobody has reread in two years. Past a thousand the mechanism shifts to calibration and the internal transfer market: people move toward the parts of the company where their behaviour is rewarded.

Say plainly what does not change. The failure protocol is invariant: punishing honest bets suppresses information everywhere, on any margin. The promotion signal is invariant. Representativeness is invariant — the enterprise and AI versions of the sampling error are the same error. Claims that consumer teams need a different culture from enterprise teams conflate the instrument, which differs, with the habit, which does not.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

Brihat, April to September 2026. Kaushik did not refuse the gate; he redimensioned it. The threshold became cost-of-being-wrong rather than build size: anything touching contracted calculations, pricing, or data not restorable from a prior state required two design-partner sessions and a reversal plan, whatever the effort; everything else shipped behind a flag with a thirty-day activation target. Of the first nineteen features, six fell in the gated class. Two were killed for ₹2.8 lakh of discovery time instead of ₹21 lakh of build. One proceeded against the sessions' advice as an override signed by Kaushik — the important artefact, because it made disagreement legible. Thirty-day activation rose from 31% to 47%.

Bhramari, April to August 2026. Farida held the launch by eight weeks, costing a ₹1.1 crore milestone payment and a difficult conversation with the client's chief operating officer. The suite was reweighted to match live traffic — code-mixed utterances from 6% to 43% — and the headline pass rate fell at once to 74.6%, which Farida published internally with the note that the number had not worsened, only become honest. Second, every product manager and engineer on the pod now hand-grades ten live calls a week, sampled proportionally by language and district. At the August relaunch the suite read 88.1% against hand-graded acceptability of 86%.

Bageecha Fresh Network: a transformation that failed. Bageecha, a Hyderabad grocery marketplace, spent FY25 converting fourteen feature teams into outcome-owning pods, each with a quarterly metric. At year end the pods claimed ₹41 crore of incremental gross merchandise value; a holdout measurement by central analytics put the figure near ₹6 crore, while contribution margin per order sat unchanged at negative ₹18.

The metrics were not additively honest. Pods could move their numbers by drawing on two shared resources — a subsidy pool and home-surface placement — so one pod's gain was often another's loss, recorded twice. Recovery took two quarters: a shared-constraint ledger in which subsidy rupees and surface slots were centrally allocated and debited to the claiming pod; holdout-measured uplift net of subsidy for any claim above ₹50 lakh; and paired reviews for pods whose metrics interacted. FY26 claimed uplift fell to ₹9 crore, measured uplift was ₹7 crore, and contribution margin improved to negative ₹4.

9. Failure modes, warnings, and the cost of catching them late

Proxy capture. A team is measured on an instrument — eval pass rate, story points, sessions logged — and optimises it. Warning: the proxy improves for two quarters while the outcome is flat. Diagnostic: if this number hit its maximum, what would a customer notice? Caught late, the cost is a full instrument rebuild plus the credibility of every decision made on the old readings.

Attribution inflation. Warning: the sum of team claims exceeds the company number. Diagnostic: what shared resource did this team draw on, and who was debited? Caught late, as at Bageecha, the cost is a year of capital spent on transfers and a board told a false story in good faith.

Evidence theatre. Artefacts are produced and archived; decisions are unchanged. Warning: the dead field. Diagnostic: name the last decision this process reversed. Caught late, the cost is cynicism, harder to repair than the process.

The captured sample. Evidence comes from whoever is easy to reach. Warning: the same four logos in every readout. Diagnostic: compare the evidence population to the served population, column by column. Caught late, the product loses the market it was built for.

Silent risk aversion. After one badly handled failure, teams stop proposing anything that could fail. Warning: roadmap items with genuinely uncertain outcomes fall below one in five and nothing has been killed in two quarters. Diagnostic: what did we stop doing this quarter, and who decided? Caught late, the cost is invisible — an orderly organisation that has stopped learning.

10. Where competent people genuinely disagree

Does culture cause performance, or does performance buy culture? Accelerate uses structural equation modelling on multi-year survey data to argue that generative culture predicts delivery and organisational performance. The counter-case is severe: the data are self-reported, respondents at successful firms rate everything favourably, and the arrow may run backwards — profitable firms can afford patient evidence, and the patience is then read as its cause. A within-firm staggered intervention would settle it; almost nobody runs one.

Empowerment against founder standards. The first holds that people closest to the problem, given outcome and context, outperform a central decider, and that the alternative stops scaling around a hundred engineers. The second, revived by the 2024 founder-mode argument, holds that taste is not distributable, that empowered organisations regress toward the defensible mediocre, and that most invocations of empowerment are leaders declining to hold a standard. Both cite conspicuous successes. They answer different questions — decision quality under uncertainty versus maintenance of a standard — and nobody has a rule for when each dominates.

Can culture be measured at all? One camp points to six-item scales with respectable psychometrics. The other holds that such instruments capture sentiment, that every proxy is gameable once it is a target, and that the only honest measurements are behavioural traces — rollback handling, promotion cases, holdout discipline — which do not aggregate into a score. The first camp runs culture programmes with dashboards; the second refuses to.

Is the build trap cultural or economic? Perri and Cagan treat feature factories as a correctable leadership failure. The Christensen reading predicts that a business whose margins cannot fund learning regenerates a feature factory however it is reorganised. The distinguishing test is seldom run: find two firms with similar margins and persistently different evidence behaviour.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this installs rituals: a discovery template, a customer clip atop the review, a blameless postmortem. Someone who has internalised it changes the rubric before the ritual, because the expensive signal outranks the cheap one. They express evidence thresholds as functions of reversibility rather than effort, and budget explicitly for false kills instead of pretending a gate has one error rate. They audit their evidence population against the served population as routine. Before endorsing a team metric they check what every team would claim against the company number. And they can say which parts of their organisation's behaviour are set by its margin structure and are therefore not available to exhortation.

12. What each of them decided

Kaushik returned to the board on 14 April with Figure 1 and one sentence: a uniform gate on a portfolio where eleven features carry ₹26 crore is negative-value above a 7.5% false-kill rate, and five interviews with institutional buyers will exceed that. He proposed the reversibility threshold instead, offered the override log as the board's audit trail, and committed to thirty-day activation as the indicator he could be held to. He also conceded that four accounts out of forty-one was a real failure.

Farida held the launch, absorbed the ₹1.1 crore slip, and published the fall from 91.2% to 74.6% under her own name. The second decision mattered more. She made the staff engineer's off-the-books sample the pod's weekly obligation, and opened the August review with the two calls the agent had handled worst. Whether that becomes a habit or an artefact will be visible in a year, in the template field nobody fills in.

Discussion questions.

  1. Kaushik's arithmetic attributes ₹26 crore of ARR to eleven features. How much of his argument survives if that attribution is half right?
  2. Farida's reweighted eval matches current traffic. What has she done to Bhramari's ability to detect a change in traffic composition next year?
  3. Where would the sum of team claims exceed your company number, and who would have to be debited for it to stop?

13. Going deeper

  • Empowered teams vs feature teams — the structural precondition for all of this; the team model sets the ceiling on culture.
  • Product transformations — changing structure, metrics and rubric together; Bageecha shows what two of the three buys.
  • Product org models — how work is split decides which metrics can be additively honest.
  • Team topologies and ownership boundaries — the seams; platform teams need a different evidence contract.
  • Managing product managers — the director layer is where culture lives between a hundred and five hundred people.
  • Hiring PMs — a slower, more durable instrument; interview loops encode standards regardless of intent.
  • PM levels and career ladders — where an organisation writes down, expensively, what it rewards.
  • Product operations — keeps evidence instruments, sampling and holdouts from drifting into fiction.

Product Culture: What It Actually Looks Like on a Tuesday

Not the mission statement on the wall — the thing a team does by reflex when no one senior is in the room.

A record quarter that made the numbers worse

On the morning of 3 March 2025, Ananya Deshpande, Vice President of Product at Ghoomti Mobility Systems, a Bengaluru-based ride-hailing and last-mile delivery platform operating in thirty-four Indian cities, opened the Q4 FY25 business review deck and found a contradiction she could not explain away. Her organisation had shipped seventeen features that quarter — parcel scheduling, a fuel-cost calculator, four payment options, a redesigned trip-tracking screen — its fastest quarter on record against a historical average of eleven. Engineering was proud of the throughput. But thirty-day rider retention, the metric Ghoomti had told its Series D investors it would defend, had fallen from 34% to 29% over two quarters, and driver Net Promoter Score was down nine points. The board's question, relayed by the CEO the previous evening, was blunt: if the team is shipping more than ever, why are the numbers getting worse?

The stakes were concrete. Ghoomti's growth covenant tied a ₹40 crore annual revenue corridor to retention holding above 32%; two more quarters at this trend would trip it. The obvious fix — hire four more product managers to ship faster — was already on the table for her sign-off by Friday. Ananya suspected it would make things worse, but lacked the language to explain why to a board that measured product health by release notes. What she was looking at, unnamed so far, was a culture problem: an organisation that had quietly optimised itself to reward the wrong thing.

The idea: culture is what a team does when no one is watching

Product culture is the shared, largely unwritten set of beliefs and habitual behaviours that determine how a product organisation actually decides — what evidence it demands before committing engineering time, whether it rewards features shipped or results moved, and whether real customers are a living presence in decisions or a persona slide dusted off twice a year. It is distinct from process, the documented steps a team is meant to follow: culture is what survives once the process document is forgotten and no executive is watching.

The vocabulary sharpened over roughly a decade. Amazon's "working backwards" discipline, formalised under Jeff Bezos from the early 2000s, forced teams to write the customer-facing press release before writing code, embedding evidence-first thinking into daily habit. Spotify's 2012 paper on "squads, tribes, and guilds" popularised autonomous, outcome-owning teams as a cultural default. Marty Cagan's writing through the Silicon Valley Product Group, especially the 2020 book Empowered, named the sharpest diagnostic: most organisations sit in what he and Melissa Perri call the "build trap" — measuring themselves by output rather than outcome, the roadmap as features to build rather than problems to solve. The sentence Ananya could eventually repeat in a board meeting without sounding glib: a product culture is revealed not by what a team says it values, but by what it will not ship without proof, and what it will happily ship without any.

How it actually works: six mechanics that add up to a culture

Ananya was tempted to look for the problem in the abstract — an engagement survey. What she needed instead was to trace six concrete mechanics that, together, constitute a product culture, and check each against how Ghoomti actually operated.

What gets measured and rewarded. Ghoomti's PM reviews scored people on "features shipped against roadmap commitment." A PM who spent six weeks proving a feature was not worth building had nothing to show at review time — the system taught PMs to ship, not to learn.

What a team must produce before it may proceed. There was no formal evidence gate. A feature could reach production without a usability test, provided an engineering estimate existed. Evidence was optional; a schedulable estimate was not.

Who is in the room when a decision gets made. Roadmap reviews held product, engineering and the CEO. No driver, no rider, no support-call transcript had entered that room in four months.

How failure is treated. The one experiment that had failed publicly that year — a surge-pricing cap trial — saw its PM quietly moved off the pricing pod. Every other PM had noticed.

How the roadmap is framed. The document was named features with ship dates, not problems ("drivers idle too long between trips in Tier-2 cities") for teams to solve as evidence pointed.

The rituals that enact all this. Standups covered ticket status; nothing in the weekly rhythm surfaced a customer's voice until the quarterly review — three months too late to course-correct.

A worked example: putting a number on the culture

To make the diagnosis legible to a board that trusted numbers, Ananya ran an audit she called the evidence ratio: of the last forty features shipped, how many had any pre-launch evidence — a usability test, an experiment, a structured interview — versus how many shipped on internal opinion alone?

QuarterFeatures shippedEvidence-backedEvidence ratioD30 retention
Q2 FY25 (baseline)11545%34%
Q3 FY2514429%31%
Q4 FY25 (audit)17635%29%
Table 1 — Ghoomti's evidence ratio, computed as evidence-backed features ÷ total shipped, tracked against thirty-day rider retention across three quarters.

The arithmetic is unforgiving: 6 ÷ 17 = 35%, meaning eleven of seventeen features that quarter reached riders and drivers with no evidence behind the decision beyond a cost estimate. Feature count had risen 55% since Q2, while the evidence ratio fell ten points and retention fell five. The correlation did not prove causation alone, but it fit a simple mechanism: a culture rewarding shipping speed over proof pushed teams toward the fast, obvious, low-risk version of an idea rather than testing whether it was the right one.

Ananya then modelled a second pass: no feature over two sprint-weeks of engineering time could ship without one piece of pre-launch evidence. Applied retroactively, nine of seventeen features would have been held back; two, prototype-tested with sixty riders in Pune and Indore, were abandoned outright — saving fourteen engineer-weeks. At Ghoomti's fully-loaded cost of roughly ₹9 lakh per sprint-week, that was about ₹1.26 crore redirectable toward the two ideas evidence said were worth pursuing.

The nuances a learner must sit with

Culture is neither process nor perks, and neither can manufacture it

A company can install OKRs and a discovery template — or free lunches and an open office — and still ship on opinion, because none of it changes what gets rewarded. Process is the visible ritual and perks are the atmosphere; culture is the incentive underneath both. Ghoomti had a discovery template nobody used past the first field.

Empowerment is not abdication, and language alone cannot install it

Handing a team a problem instead of a feature works only if leadership sets a clear outcome target and holds the team accountable for it; without that, "empowerment" is leadership declining to decide, and teams drift toward whatever ships easiest. Telling teams to "think like owners" while keeping a features-not-problems roadmap changes nothing — the org chart and incentives must move first, or the new language is theatre.

Evidence over opinion does not mean data over judgment

In a genuinely new market, there may be no data yet; a founder's informed judgment is itself evidence. What matters is whether the organisation later tests that judgment against reality.

Outcomes over output can be gamed just as easily as output can

A team told to move a retention number can do so briefly with a discount that borrows growth from next quarter. A healthy outcome culture pairs the target metric with a guardrail — Ghoomti later added a complaint-rate ceiling — so the win cannot be manufactured at the customer's expense.

"Customers in the room" is not the same as customer worship

In B2B products, the loudest voice is often the largest account's request, amplified by a sales team with a quota. A genuine culture weighs that voice against a broader evidence base rather than treating it as automatically decisive.

Culture cannot tell you whether the strategy is right

A team can be evidence-driven and customer-present, and still build for a market about to be disrupted. Culture governs how well an organisation learns; it is not a substitute for judgment about what is worth learning.

How it differs by product type and by company stage

In consumer products such as Ghoomti's rider app, evidence is abundant and cheap — reviews, in-app data, thousands of tickets — so a weak culture is a discipline failure: the evidence exists and simply is not being looked at. In B2B products, evidence is scarcer and more political; the "customer in the room" is filtered through account managers and a handful of design partners, so a healthy culture must work harder to hear the silent majority who never call anyone. In marketplace products the question doubles, because two sides — riders and drivers — can be pulled in opposite directions by the same feature, so evidence must be weighed on both before a change counts as a success.

Stage matters just as much. Early-stage, culture is largely the founder's own habits, since there is no institutional memory to override. In a large organisation, culture becomes a function of what middle management measures and promotes on, since most PMs never interact with the founder — exactly the layer where Ghoomti's problem lived, in a rubric no executive had examined in two years.

Common mistakes

Mistaking velocity for health. Symptom: leadership celebrates a record quarter of ship counts. Misunderstanding: output as a proxy for outcome. Diagnostic: plot feature count against the true-north metric, as Table 1 does; a rising line crossing a falling one is the tell.

Writing values nobody is measured against. Symptom: a "customer obsession" value on the careers page, no customer voice in any recurring ritual. Misunderstanding: culture treated as a statement, not a reward system. Diagnostic: ask the last five people promoted what got them promoted.

Punishing the wrong failure. Symptom: the PM who ran an honest experiment that failed gets quietly sidelined, as at Ghoomti. Misunderstanding: leaders confuse a failed experiment with a failed PM. Diagnostic: check whether the last killed idea's owner was promoted or moved out within two quarters.

Confusing empowerment with silence. Symptom: teams given "full ownership" but no outcome target, drifting toward whatever ships easiest. Misunderstanding: leadership believes stepping back equals empowering. Diagnostic: ask three team leads what number their team owns this quarter; mismatched answers mean ownership was never granted.

What good looks like

Picture the same decision six months later, handled the way Amazon's writing culture or Spotify's squad model was designed to force. A team proposing a feature first writes a one-page brief: who is affected, what evidence shows the problem is real, and what it costs to be wrong. A small, cheap test — a prototype in front of fifteen users, an experiment flagged to 2% of traffic — runs before engineering time is committed. The weekly review opens with a customer clip before any roadmap slide appears. When an experiment fails, the retro asks what was learned, and the PM presents the finding with no dip in standing. The roadmap is problems ranked by impact, teams free to propose the solution, not features with dates attached. None of this needs budget; it needs the reward system, roadmap format and weekly ritual to point one direction.

What Ananya decided, and what comes next

Ananya did not ask the board for more product managers. She asked for two changes defensible with Table 1 alone: an evidence gate for anything over two sprint-weeks of engineering effort, and a rewrite of the PM rubric so a well-run experiment that correctly killed a bad idea counted as much as a shipped feature. She kept the quarterly review, but opened it with unedited driver and rider verbatims before any feature slide appeared. None of this promised immediate recovery; it promised that the next seventeen features shipped would be ones the organisation had reason to believe in, and that the next time a number moved, the causal story would be visible rather than argued over afterward.

The natural next step is product transformations — the harder discipline of changing an organisation's culture, structure and metrics at once, under more pressure than Ananya had, across teams that did not choose the change. Everything here describes a healthy culture once it exists; a transformation is the messier work of getting an unhealthy one to become it. Two questions worth sitting with: what decision on your team shipped last with no evidence behind it? And if you audited your own last twenty decisions as Ananya audited Ghoomti's forty, what would your evidence ratio be — and would you want that number in front of your board?

Unmesh Systems: What the Roadmap Rewards

A case for discussion

1. Bengaluru, 25 September 2026

Ananya Rao, Vice-President of Product at Unmesh Systems, read the same Slack thread for the third time. It was 9:40 p.m. In eleven days the board would meet to approve the FY27 Q3 roadmap review, and forty minutes before that meeting Ananya would join a renewal call with Khalid Al Mansoori, VP of Customer Experience at Unmesh's largest account, a retail conglomerate in Dubai. Khalid wanted to know whether three promised features — a WhatsApp Business API escalation flow, a custom SLA dashboard, and a direct ERP sync — would ship on schedule. Ananya did not yet know what she would tell him, because she had just finished a memo from her design lead in Berlin arguing that the roadmap itself was the problem.

2. A company built on speed

Unmesh Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2016 by two engineers who had left Freshworks to build a lighter, faster customer-support platform for small and mid-sized businesses. Its product, Setu, combined ticketing, chat and an AI-assisted response layer, and it grew the way many Indian SaaS companies grow: founder-led sales for two years, then a Series C in 2022 that funded expansion into Southeast Asia and the Gulf. By FY27, Unmesh served roughly 1,390 customers — D2C retailers, fintech support desks, hospital front offices — competing against Freshworks, Zoho Desk and a scatter of regional players, on total annual recurring revenue of ₹196 crore. Its pitch to investors had always been the same: Unmesh shipped faster than rivals its size, because product managers worked directly off customer requests rather than committee-built specs. That instinct had won its most prized account eighteen months earlier — the Dubai retail group, brought in by sales head Tom Bradley, worth ₹17.2 crore in annual recurring revenue and, to the board, proof that Unmesh could win outside India.

3. What Ananya knew

Over the past three quarters, that instinct had hardened into a habit. Feature requests from Unmesh's dozen largest accounts, led by the Dubai group, now went almost directly from Tom's sales team to engineering manager Rohan Iyer in Pune, with product managers writing PRDs to match commitments already made on client calls. Features shipped each quarter had risen from 18 to 27, and at the last all-hands that number was read out to applause. But Naveen Chandrasekaran, the data scientist tracking product analytics from Toronto, had sent Ananya a dashboard two weeks earlier showing that the self-serve small-business segment — 1,240 of Unmesh's 1,390 customers, and half its revenue — was quietly coming apart: usage down, conversion down, churn up. Grace Lim, running customer success from Singapore, had been raising the same worry in writing since July, without much response. Mara Fischer, the design lead in Berlin, had spent her own time in August interviewing eleven churned small-business customers; none mentioned wanting the features Unmesh had spent the quarter building. Nobody had set out to build a feature factory. But the metric the company now celebrated was output, and the customers in the room, increasingly, were the loudest ones, not the most representative ones.

4. The people

Tom Bradley, Head of Global Sales, New Jersey. Wants the Dubai renewal signed and the three promised features delivered on the dates his team committed to. Argues that Unmesh's growth story depends on a small number of large, visible accounts, and that slowing down to "run research" now would look like the company losing its nerve just as the Gulf expansion is proving out.

Mara Fischer, Lead Product Designer, Berlin. Wants discovery reinstated as a gate before anything enters the roadmap. Has evidence, from her own interviews, that the small-business segment is churning for reasons the roadmap has never addressed, and believes the product organisation has stopped asking customers what they need before building for them.

Grace Lim, Director of Customer Success, Singapore. Wants the roadmap to reflect the whole customer base, not just its biggest accounts. Renews and rescues at-risk customers across India, Southeast Asia and the Gulf, and is the person who has to explain, quarter after quarter, why a customer's basic requests were never prioritised.

Khalid Al Mansoori, VP Customer Experience, Dubai retail group. Wants the three committed features delivered as promised, and wants a straight answer on the call. Has been a fair and patient client, but has also told Tom that if Unmesh cannot deliver what it agreed to, his team will start evaluating Freshworks.

5. What the numbers showed

Ananya pulled up two exhibits before the call. Exhibit 1, built from Naveen's dashboard, showed three quarters of decline beneath three quarters of apparent progress.

Exhibit 1 — Unmesh Systems, quarterly product metrics (last three quarters)

Source: Unmesh Systems product analytics and finance, internal. SMB = small-business self-serve segment.

Exhibit 2 showed where engineering time actually went that quarter, set against where the revenue actually sat.

Exhibit 2 — Revenue and Q3 engineering capacity, by segment

Dubai account alone: ₹17.2 crore ARR (8.8% of total), roughly one-fifth of Q3 enterprise-track engineering capacity.

Read together, the two exhibits said the same thing twice. A segment holding half of Unmesh's revenue and nearly all its customers was losing engagement while receiving a quarter of engineering attention; a segment holding a sixth of revenue, anchored by one account, absorbed more than half. The roadmap did not reflect the business — it reflected whoever asked most recently and most loudly.

Exhibit 3 — the current single-file path from account request to shipped code (top), against a two-track, evidence-gated flow with a feedback loop back to customer signal (bottom).

6. The options

A. Keep the sales-led roadmap

Confirm the three Dubai commitments, formalise account-based feature planning for two more quarters, and keep "features shipped" as the metric the board sees. This protects the ₹17.2 crore renewal and the growth story the board already believes, but locks in the current split of engineering time and leaves no answer for Naveen's and Mara's evidence, or for the ₹98 crore self-serve segment now shrinking in front of her.

B. Pivot immediately to an outcomes-only model

Suspend new one-off enterprise commitments, put every team on quarterly outcome OKRs, and require every PRD to cite discovery evidence before entering the roadmap. This directly answers Mara's and Naveen's findings and could show improvement in the self-serve segment within two quarters. It also means walking into the Dubai call without firm delivery dates, risking the account and the story it tells the board about Unmesh's readiness for global accounts, nine days before that board meets.

C. Two protected tracks, gated by evidence

Split roadmap capacity into a core track governed by outcome metrics and discovery evidence, and a smaller enterprise-solutions track for account requests that pass an evidence gate — proof of reusable value beyond one client, not just size of the account. Honour the three Dubai commitments already made, but require every future enterprise ask to clear the same bar as everything else. Review outcome metrics monthly with sales and customer success in the room, using recorded customer calls as evidence. This preserves the Dubai relationship near-term while changing what the roadmap rewards, at the cost of slower change than Option B and real discipline to keep the gate from quietly reopening into Option A.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, read together, actually reveal about Unmesh's product culture — is the problem the Dubai account, or what the organisation has chosen to measure and reward?
  2. Each stakeholder — Tom, Mara, Grace, Khalid — has evidence or experience the others lack. What would it mean, practically, to bring "the customer" into this decision, given that Unmesh's customers disagree with each other about what matters?
  3. Compare Options A, B and C on one criterion at a time: revenue risk in the next quarter, credibility with the board, and long-run health of the self-serve segment. Does any option win on all three?
  4. If Ananya chooses Option C, what exactly must she say to Khalid on the renewal call, and what must she say to Tom before that call, for the new gate to hold?

8. A note for the learner

Product culture is not a values poster; it is whatever the roadmap actually rewards. Unmesh's leadership never voted to become a feature factory — it kept score by output instead of outcomes, and let the loudest customer stand in for the whole base. That is how healthy-looking companies drift: the metric easiest to report at a town hall wins, evidence that takes longer to gather loses, and "customers in the room" quietly comes to mean the biggest account rather than a representative one.

A well-reasoned answer does not treat evidence-based culture as a purity test that forces Ananya to burn the Dubai relationship to prove a point, nor does it treat the renewal as an excuse to leave the incentive system unchanged. Option A ignores evidence Ananya has already seen and cannot unsee. Option B applies the right principle so abruptly it creates a new, avoidable crisis nine days before the board meets, for a gain almost as reachable under an orderly transition. Option C is the defensible path: it uses evidence to change what enters the roadmap and how it is judged, keeps faith with an existing commitment, and makes the customers in the room — plural, weighted by more than volume of Slack messages — a structural feature of planning rather than a slogan. Product Org Models: Outcome, Component, Segment, Platform

How should product teams be organised — and what changes, in the work itself, when a company answers that question one way rather than another?

1. A Monday morning in Bengaluru

On 9 February 2026, Priya Deshmukh, SVP of Product at Manas Product Cloud, a Bengaluru-headquartered analytics platform sold to mid-market finance teams, opened the quarterly review deck she would present to the board that Thursday. Manas had grown to $28 million in annual recurring revenue, 340 customers across India, the US and the UK, 96 engineers and 22 product managers. One number on the third slide had not moved in three straight quarters: activation — new customers reaching their first working dashboard within 14 days — was stuck at 46%. Below 55%, the company's data showed, odds of renewing at year one fell by roughly a third.

Priya's organisation was structured, as it had been since 2021, around eleven "component pods" — Ingestion, Transform, Dashboards, Alerts, Search, Permissions, Billing, Mobile, Integrations, Reporting, Notifications — each with its own PM, designer and six to eight engineers. Every pod owned a slice of the technical system; no pod owned activation. Pulling the ticket history, she found the same pattern in feature after feature: a new customer's first 14 days touched five of the eleven pods, and each hand-off sat in a queue for days before anyone picked it up. Nobody was late; nobody was underperforming — the org chart was producing the delay. Priya had six weeks before the board meeting, and her choice would shape how roughly 120 people worked for the next two years.

2. The idea

A product org model is the rule a company uses to decide what each product team owns and is accountable for moving. It answers one deceptively simple question: when boxes are drawn on an org chart and a PM put in charge of each, what is the boundary of that box — an outcome, a piece of technology, a group of customers, or a shared capability? Four answers recur often enough to have names. An outcome team owns a metric — activation, retention, expansion revenue — with authority to change whatever moves it, wherever in the codebase that work lives. A component team owns a piece of the stack — a search service, a billing engine — regardless of which outcome is served that week. A segment team owns a customer group, usually by size, vertical or geography, serving the full product to it. A platform team owns shared infrastructure — a design system, a data pipeline — built once so other teams need not build their own.

The problem is older than the product-management title itself. In 1967 computer scientist Melvin Conway observed that any organisation designing a system produces a design mirroring its own communication structure — Conway's Law. If five teams each own a slice of a customer journey, that journey will feel built by five teams, seams at every hand-off, whatever the individual teams' skill. Amazon's "two-pizza team" doctrine, from the early 2000s, fixed this with small, end-to-end accountable teams; Spotify's 2012 paper on "squads" and "tribes," by Henrik Kniberg and Anders Ivarsson, popularised outcome-oriented autonomous teams as a copyable pattern. The most rigorous synthesis is Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais's 2019 book Team Topologies, naming four types — stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem — and arguing most organisations should default to stream-aligned teams, adding the rest only where they demonstrably cut cognitive load. Priya's boardroom sentence: "We organise around the outcomes we most need to move, and build platform teams only where shared infrastructure is cheaper to build once than to duplicate five times."

Fig. 1 — The four axes along which a product organisation can be cut. Most companies mix at least two: an outcome or segment layer atop a thin platform layer.

3. How it actually works

Choosing an org model is a sequence of five steps; practitioners most often skip the second and fourth. First, inventory the handful of outcomes that genuinely determine trajectory — for Manas, activation, retention, expansion; resist naming more than four or five, since an outcome owned by nobody in particular is a slogan, not an outcome. Second, usually skipped: inventory the technical components and mark honestly which are shared by two or more outcomes versus used by only one — this tells a company whether it can afford pure outcome teams or needs platform teams underneath. Third, inventory the customer segments that differ enough in need to require genuinely different product decisions, not just different sales pitches. Fourth, also usually skipped: map current teams against all three inventories and flag every place ownership is ambiguous or duplicated — that ambiguity, not incompetence, is usually the real cause of the slow features executives complain about. Fifth, choose one primary axis, since a company can only have one without recreating the coordination problem it is solving. Review roughly every twelve to twenty-four months or whenever headcount doubles, since the right cut at 40 engineers is rarely right at 150.

4. A worked example, with the arithmetic shown

Priya's team had two quarters of ticket data: 41 tickets needed a hand-off between component pods to ship one change, and the average sat in a receiving pod's backlog for 6.1 days before anyone started it, regardless of urgency. A typical activation feature — a smarter default dashboard for new users — touched five pods: Ingestion, Transform, Dashboards, Permissions, Billing. Engineering work ran about 15 days once assigned. The arithmetic for the current structure:
