Component model (current)530.51545.5 days ≈ 6.5 weeks

Priya modelled an alternative: a nine-person Activation team — one PM, one designer, seven engineers — with authority to change ingestion display, transform rules, dashboard layout and permission defaults directly, without waiting on four other pods. The only genuine shared dependency was the core data-ingestion pipeline, used by nine other areas and kept as a small platform team rather than duplicated nine times. The feature now touches one dependency, not four:

StructureExternal dependenciesHand-off queue days (1×6.1)Build daysTotal elapsed
Outcome model (proposed)16.11521.1 days ≈ 3.0 weeks

That first pass makes the outcome model look unambiguously better — roughly 54% faster. Priya then changed one input: what if the feature also needed a billing-logic change, billing being a second shared platform capability five other outcome teams depended on? With two dependencies instead of one, the queue cost becomes 2 × 6.1 = 12.2 days, a total of 27.2 days, or 3.9 weeks — still faster than 6.5 weeks, but the margin has shrunk by a third, and keeps shrinking with every dependency the team cannot absorb. Outcome teams do not eliminate coordination cost; they concentrate it onto however many platform dependencies remain, which is why the honest inventory must happen before the chart is redrawn, not after.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

An "outcome team" is not the same as a "feature team"

A feature team is assigned a roadmap slice and disbands once it ships; an outcome team is durable, accountable for a metric over years — which gives it standing to say no to a feature that would not move it. Confusing the two yields outcome-team titles with feature-team incentives.

Platform teams need customers, not just consumers

A platform team that treats other teams as captive users rather than customers whose time it must earn tends to build capability nobody adopts. The healthiest, at firms like Atlassian and Razorpay, run something close to an internal product practice, with roadmaps and satisfaction surveys.

Segment cuts can quietly become component cuts

A segment team serving "Enterprise" often ends up owning enterprise-only technical features — SSO, audit logs — and drifts into a component team wearing a segment label. The tell: is its roadmap driven by what enterprise customers need this quarter, or a fixed list nobody revisits?

Reorg cadence is a real cost, not a free lever

Every switch of axis costs roughly one to two quarters of reduced velocity while people relearn who owns what and rebuild trust across new boundaries. A company reorganising annually because leadership keeps finding "a better model" usually loses more to churn than any structure gains it.

Ownership and authority must travel together

Giving a team a metric to own while another retains veto power over the code that moves it is not an outcome model but a component model with extra reporting. The real question is not what a team is named but what it can ship without asking permission.

What it cannot tell you

The framework says nothing about whether the chosen outcomes are right, or how to treat cases — privacy, security, financial controls — where centralised control is a compliance requirement, not a preference.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early-stage versus scaled

The choice bends with the kind of product. Consumer products with a single, large, homogeneous user base — a Swiggy or a Spotify — lean toward pure outcome teams, since there is usually no reason to split the audience into segments. B2B products with different needs by size or vertical, as Manas discovered, often need a segment layer above the outcome layer: an enterprise-serving and an SMB-serving team for the same metric can legitimately make different trade-offs, since a large bank's activation journey and a small accounting firm's are not the same problem. Marketplaces carry an extra axis — supply and demand are different customers — so firms like Flipkart or Uber typically run separate outcome teams for sellers and buyers, plus a platform layer for shared matching and payments infrastructure. Stage matters as much as product type: a ten-person startup does not need this framework, since with one team the question is moot, and imposing structure prematurely is itself a mistake. Somewhere between 30 and 80 engineers, hand-off delays start appearing; past a few hundred, almost every company runs a hybrid, since single-axis models rarely survive real scale.

7. Common mistakes

Reorganising around outcomes without building the platform first. Symptom: five new outcome teams each rebuilding their own authentication or notifications within two quarters. Misunderstanding: treating the component inventory as optional. Diagnostic: count teams already building near-identical capability, then multiply once they move independently.

Declaring outcome ownership without matching authority. Symptom: an "Activation team" still filing a ticket with Dashboards to change the dashboard. Misunderstanding: confusing a new title with a new operating agreement. Diagnostic: ask the PM to name the last three changes shipped needing no other team's time — none means the chart changed, not the work.

Copying a well-known company's structure without checking conditions hold. Symptom: a 60-person firm running Spotify's tribe-and-chapter model and finding it mostly adds meetings. Misunderstanding: treating an org model as best practice rather than the answer to conditions that may not yet exist. Diagnostic: has the company hit the symptom the model fixes, or pre-empted one it doesn't have?

Reorganising too often. Symptom: staff who recite three prior structures from memory and treat the current one as provisional. Misunderstanding: believing a better model found sooner outweighs the relearning cost each switch imposes. Diagnostic: has the structure had at least a year against the metrics it was meant to move?

8. What good looks like

Six months after Priya's reorganisation, Manas ran three outcome teams — Activation, Retention, Expansion — each with clear metric ownership and authority to change any part of the product their outcome touched. Underneath sat two genuinely shared platform teams, Data Pipeline and Identity, staffed because two or more outcome teams demonstrably needed the same capability, not because platform teams sounded impressive on a chart. The enterprise segment, distinct enough to warrant it, kept a small team layered atop Activation and Retention rather than duplicating them. Every team could name its metric and its dependencies in one sentence — none more than two. Activation rose from 46% to 61% in two quarters, and the hand-off count behind a typical feature fell from five to an average of 1.4.

9. What Priya decided, and two questions to sit with

Priya proposed, and the board approved, a move from eleven component pods to three outcome teams atop two platform teams and one enterprise segment team — a hybrid, arrived at only after the component inventory told her which two capabilities were worth centralising and which nine were not. She next asked her leads to study Team Topologies' distinction between platform and "enabling" teams, since her next problem — helping outcome teams that lacked data-engineering skill actually use Data Pipeline well — was a different failure mode, calling for a different kind of team.

Two questions worth sitting with:

First — can any team in your organisation name, without checking, the last change it shipped that required no other team's engineering time? Second — if you audited your shared components as honestly as Priya's did, how many would survive being called "genuinely shared," and how many are shared only because nobody has yet argued for giving one team clear ownership?

Zaroorat Finance Cloud: Which Org Model Wins the Enterprise Desk?

Bengaluru, Monday, 28 September 2026. Ananya Rao, VP of Product at Zaroorat Finance Cloud, closed her laptop after a call with the company's largest customer — a Dubai-listed ports-and-logistics group whose finance controller had, for the third month running, asked when the platform would let his Jebel Ali office file input-VAT returns without a manual spreadsheet reconciliation. Ananya had eleven days before the leadership offsite in Goa, where the board expected a firm recommendation on how the 42-person product and engineering organisation should be structured. Three plans sat in her draft folder; she had to choose one and defend it to a team spread across four time zones.

1. Company background

Zaroorat Finance Cloud sells software Indian companies use to manage employee travel, expenses and corporate card spending — a category also served by Zoho Expense, SAP Concur and Happay. Founded in Bengaluru in 2018 by two former Razorpay engineers, Zaroorat built its name on a rules engine that auto-classified expense lines against GST input-credit eligibility, a problem most rivals handled with manual tagging. By September 2026 the company had 380 employees, ₹42.7 crore in annual recurring revenue, and roughly 2,400 customers from ten-person startups to listed manufacturers. Its card-issuing product ran on rails from a partner bank and Razorpay, and its ledger engine was the system many customers' auditors relied on at year-end.

Through 2024 and 2025, growth came almost entirely from SMBs buying the self-serve product off the website. In early 2026, under investor pressure to show enterprise traction, the company signed nine large GCC accounts — Indian conglomerates' regional finance arms wanting one platform across headquarters and Gulf subsidiaries. That push opened a second front: multi-currency ledgers, UAE VAT invoicing, and data-residency questions the product had never faced for a purely domestic, DPDP Act-governed base.

2. The situation

The immediate trigger was a board metric everyone now watched: median time from a qualified enterprise feature request to shipped release. For SMB customers this was under three weeks. For the forty accounts in the enterprise and GCC segment it had drifted to 132 days, and the Dubai client's VAT-filing request had been waiting 96 of those. Ananya's product organisation was structured by technical component — Core Ledger, Cards & Payments, Mobile, and Integrations & API — each led by a strong engineering manager and optimised for its own backlog. A large enterprise request typically touched three of the four teams, and each team prioritised it below its own roadmap.

Rohan Mehta, Head of Engineering in Pune, saw the 132-day number as a prioritisation failure, not a structural one: sequence the component teams' work more clearly, he argued, and the number would fall without reorganising. Priya Iyer, running customer success from Singapore, disagreed — she had watched three teams each tell the Dubai controller his request was "in the queue," with no one able to commit a date. From Berlin, designer Elena Krause flagged a second cost: without a single owner per journey, the SMB app and enterprise console had begun to diverge visually, confusing shared users. Toronto-based data scientist Wei Chen, who built the compliance models shared across every product line, warned Ananya privately that splitting ledger and compliance logic apart to speed up one segment would be dangerous: GST e-invoicing and UAE VAT rules both touched the same tax engine, and duplicating it anywhere was a compliance risk, not a convenience.

3. The people

Rohan Mehta — Head of Engineering, Pune. Built the component teams; fears reorganisation will fragment the codebase and duplicate the ledger and compliance core.

Priya Iyer — Head of Customer Success, Singapore, covering the GCC book. Wants one accountable owner for the enterprise relationship so no customer hears three different answers.

Elena Krause — Lead Product Designer, Berlin. Wants teams organised around a coherent user journey, not technical layers.

Rajiv Bhandari — Head of Sales, New Jersey, closing Gulf and North American logos. Wants a dedicated enterprise roadmap to sell against, and is the loudest voice for segment-first.

4. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows why the enterprise and GCC segment, small in account count, could not be an afterthought: it carried higher net revenue retention than either other segment, meaning existing accounts were expanding fast even as feature delivery to them stalled.

Exhibit 2 shows why: enterprise requests rarely lived inside one team's boundary. 5. The options

Option A — Reorganise fully by customer segment

Dissolve the component teams and form three cross-functional pods — SMB, Mid-market, and Enterprise & GCC — each with its own product manager, engineers and a slice of design and data science, owning its roadmap end to end. Upside: Priya's customers get one accountable team; Rajiv can sell a named roadmap. Cost: the ledger, GST e-invoicing logic and the emerging UAE VAT engine each get rebuilt or forked inside at least two pods, multiplying compliance risk exactly where Wei Chen warned against it, and tripling the surface area the company must keep correct under DPDP Act and GST audit requirements.

Option B — Keep component teams, add a temporary enterprise task force

Leave the four component teams as they are, and fund a rotating six-person "Enterprise & GCC Readiness" squad for two quarters, borrowing engineers from each component team to unblock the top forty accounts. Upside: minimal disruption, fast to stand up, Rohan's architecture untouched. Cost: it treats a structural bottleneck as a staffing problem; the squad's engineers stay evaluated by their home managers, reproducing the split loyalty and quiet deprioritisation Priya had already seen, and the fix would likely need renewing indefinitely rather than resolving.

Option C — Split into a platform team and two outcome pods

Consolidate Core Ledger and Integrations & API into one Platform team owning the shared ledger, compliance engine and ERP/VAT connectors as an internal product with its own release cadence. Form two new outcome-owning pods — Growth (SMB activation) and Enterprise & GCC (expansion and retention) — each with a product manager and engineers, drawing extra platform capacity through a quarterly capacity-sharing agreement. Upside: compliance and ledger logic stays single-sourced as GCC rules multiply, while the Enterprise & GCC pod gets a named owner for the 132-day problem. Cost: stand-up takes one to two quarters, Rohan must release engineers into a shared queue, and the company must run a governance mechanism — the capacity-sharing agreement — it has never needed before.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does the 132-day figure in Exhibit 2 tell you about where the current component structure breaks down for enterprise requests?
  2. Whose incentives change under each option, and how would Rohan, Priya and Rajiv behave differently as a result?
  3. Why does Wei Chen's warning about the ledger and compliance engine matter more for Zaroorat than for a company selling only inside India?
  4. If you were Ananya Rao, which option would you take to Goa, and what risk would you tell the board you were choosing not to take?

7. A note for the learner

Product org-model choices are usually framed as a menu: organise by outcome, by component, by segment, or by platform. This case is built to expose the mistake of treating that menu as mutually exclusive. Zaroorat's real question was not "segment or component" but which parts needed segment-level ownership to move fast, and which needed to stay single-sourced because getting them wrong — a duplicated tax rule under GST or UAE VAT — was a compliance failure, not a delay.

A well-reasoned answer starts from Exhibit 2, not from Rajiv's or Priya's preference: which team is genuinely on the critical path of the board's metric, and is the fix ownership (who is accountable) or capacity (who has enough engineers)? Option B answers only capacity; Option A answers only ownership, at the cost of the compliance risk Exhibit 1's GCC growth makes newly serious.

The defensible path is Option C. It gives the Enterprise & GCC segment what Priya and Rajiv actually need — a named, accountable pod measured on the segment's own retention number — without forking the ledger and compliance engine Wei Chen identifies as a single point of regulatory truth across two tax jurisdictions. Its real cost is organisational: Rohan gives up sole control of engineers he trained, and the company must learn a capacity-sharing agreement it has never needed before — manageable against an indefinite staffing patch (Option B) or a compliance engine duplicated across fast-moving pods just as GCC rules multiply (Option A). A strong response names that trade-off explicitly rather than presenting Option C as costless.

Jaanch Inspection Cloud: Seventy-Four People, Four Org Charts, One Board Meeting

1. Thursday night, 1 October 2026 — Coimbatore

The last shuttle from the Jaanch Inspection Cloud office on Avinashi Road left at 9:40 p.m., and Anuradha Varadarajan let it go. On her desk were four printouts, each a different shape of the same seventy-four people: the product organisation she had built over five years and now had eight days to redraw. The board met on Friday, 9 October. Her co-founder and chief executive, Pradeep Nallasamy, wanted one slide — “the structure, not the options” — by Monday morning.

Two things had happened that week, and only one was on the agenda. On Tuesday, Dr Suchitra Rane, VP of Manufacturing Excellence at Dhaatu Precision Forgings — Jaanch's largest customer, ₹11.4 crore of subscription revenue across nineteen plants in Chakan, Querétaro and Gliwice — had written to say that the dedicated engineering pod promised under clause 7.4 of their 2023 master agreement had, by her count, delivered three of eleven committed items, and that renewal on 31 January 2027 would be “a conversation, not a formality”. On Wednesday, Tanvi Chaudhari, principal data scientist in Montreal, sent two lines at 3 a.m. Indian time: the defect models for the Gliwice line could not be retrained on operator-visible frames, the plant's works council having refused image retention, and nobody owned the problem of a model that had to work without the data it was designed for.

Anuradha had a whiteboard marker in her hand and no answer. What she wrote instead, and photographed, was a question: which of these four charts is about our customers, and which is about us?

2. Company history: one decision that still binds

Jaanch was founded in 2016 by Pradeep Nallasamy, a former TCS manufacturing-practice consultant, and Karthik Balasubramanian, an embedded-systems engineer, after a Coimbatore pump-castings unit told them it rejected ₹40 lakh of finished goods a year because end-of-line inspection was done by tired human eyes on a rotating shift. Their first product was a camera rig and a laptop. By 2019 it was a subscription: cameras on the line, an edge box running Jaanch's inspection runtime, a shop-floor app for supervisors, and a dashboard plant heads could show at the Monday quality review.

The decision that shaped everything came in March 2021. Rather than build its own imaging hardware, Jaanch signed a five-year exclusive supply and co-development agreement with Darpan Vision Devices of Ahmedabad: Darpan modules only, minimum offtake 18,000 units a year, ₹4.6 crore shortfall penalty, in exchange for firmware access and pricing that undercut imported systems by roughly 60 per cent. It ran to 31 March 2027. It also meant one runtime, compiled for one module family, maintained by one team — Karthik's. Every product Jaanch shipped afterwards sat on top of it.

In 2022 Dakshin Bridge Capital, a Chennai-and-Singapore growth fund, led a ₹96 crore round on a thesis of “India's Tier-2 factory floor, then their global plants”. In 2023 came the Dhaatu master agreement, which won the logo and conceded clause 7.4. In 2025 Jaanch launched a self-serve tier: two cameras, one line, ₹28,000 a month, no implementation project. By September 2026 revenue was ₹138 crore — ₹58 crore subscription, ₹61 crore hardware and installation, ₹19 crore services and maintenance — across 412 plants and 180 companies, with 263 employees.

3. The industry

Jaanch sold into the part of Indian manufacturing that had recently discovered it was being measured. Production-linked incentive schemes had pulled component makers into supply chains that audited them quarterly; Tata Motors, Mahindra, Ather and Ola Electric each ran supplier scorecards where parts-per-million defect rates moved business between vendors. GST e-invoicing had already taught the same firms that a compliance mandate could become a software purchase. Above Jaanch sat the global automation incumbents — Siemens, Rockwell, Cognex — technically superior and priced for plants ten times larger. Beside it sat Jugalbandi Automation of Pune, which bundled inspection into line-automation projects and won on its service engineers, and a long tail of integrators assembling camera kits for a third of Jaanch's price.

Two regulatory currents mattered more than any competitor. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had made worker imagery a consent question inside India, which most customers handled with a notice on the shop-floor board. Outside India it was harder: in Indian manufacturers' European plants, retaining frames showing identifiable operators required works-council agreement that was, in Gliwice, simply not forthcoming. Meanwhile European buyers had begun asking for part-level traceability records Jaanch's system could produce but had never been architected to certify. Freshworks and Zoho had shown from Chennai and Tenkasi that a product company could be built in Tamil Nadu on global standards; Jaanch's investors quoted both, often.

4. The situation in detail

Exhibit 2 lays out the sequence. Each step had been defensible at the time; several had since turned out to rest on a belief that was wrong.

Exhibit 2. Reconstructed by the product-operations team from board decks and contract dates, September 2026. The 2024 entry has no board-deck reference; it was added from Shalini Menon's trip notes.

Through 2024 the organisation ran on five component teams (Exhibit 1) and it worked, because the product was one product. Component ownership plus a strong field organisation would scale, the thinking went: Sameer Kulkarni's eighty-one deployment engineers absorbed whatever the product could not do, billed it, and everyone's numbers looked good. In FY25 services revenue grew 44 per cent — read internally as evidence of customer commitment.

By mid-2025 the self-serve tier exposed the first crack. Small suppliers churned not because inspection failed but because onboarding assumed an engineer on site. The fix — a guided setup flow — needed the runtime to self-configure, the app to change, and a general-purpose starter model. It took five months and four of the five teams.

By early 2026 the second crack was contractual. Clause 7.4's six-engineer pod existed on paper: six people whose names appeared on the Dhaatu review deck and whose sprints were set by their component managers. Dr Rane's eleven committed items included three that were, in engineering terms, platform changes affecting all 412 plants. Nobody would make them for one customer; nobody told her that.

What had turned out wrong was the diagnosis everybody agreed on in March 2026: that Jaanch had a prioritisation problem. A quarterly sequencing exercise ran from April, and Exhibit 3's cycle times improved. Yet in the same period the ARR flagged renewal-at-risk rose from ₹9.7 crore to ₹19.3 crore (Exhibit 5). The two numbers moved in opposite directions, and the reason is visible only in Exhibit 6's footnote.

5. The people

Anuradha Varadarajan — SVP Product, Coimbatore. Owns the recommendation. Believes structure should follow the customer, but cannot say which customer. Not saying: two of her four charts were drawn to be rejected, and she no longer knows which two.

Pradeep Nallasamy — Co-founder and CEO, Coimbatore. Wants a structure he can describe to the board in one sentence. Incentive: a Series C conversation opening in January. Not saying: Dakshin Bridge has asked him privately whether the company needs a chief product officer hired from outside.

Karthik Balasubramanian — Co-founder and VP Engineering, Edge & Devices, Coimbatore. Argues the runtime is the company and must stay single-sourced under one team; cites the Darpan offtake commitment as proof that hardware and firmware decisions cannot be distributed. Not saying: he has quietly been building a second runtime for a non-Darpan module family, without a mandate, against the exclusivity lapsing in March 2027.

Aparna Deshmukh — Director of Product, Shop-floor Applications, Hyderabad. Wants three outcome pods — first-pass yield, line uptime, traceability — each with its own metric. Incentive: she would lead one. Not saying: her fourteen-person team includes nine people whose week is mostly install support, and outcome pods would expose that.

Sameer Kulkarni — Head of Field Deployment & Services, Pune. Wants segment-aligned teams so his large-account engineers have someone to escalate to. Incentive: his P&L carries a 34 per cent gross margin on custom deployment work. Not saying: a product that configured itself would remove roughly ₹6 crore of that revenue, and he has not modelled what that does to eighty-one jobs.

Vikram Chidambaram — Chief Revenue Officer, Detroit. Wants a Global Accounts unit with its own roadmap and its own engineers, arguing that Jaanch's next ₹100 crore comes from Indian manufacturers' overseas plants. Not saying: he negotiated clause 7.4, and a Global Accounts unit would make him, not Anuradha, the owner of the promise.

Tanvi Chaudhari — Principal Data Scientist, Montreal. Insists the model and data pipeline must stay one shared platform; a fully loaded Montreal data scientist costs ₹78 lakh a year against ₹25 lakh in Hyderabad, so duplication across pods is arithmetically impossible. Not saying: her team is three people, is already the longest queue in the company, and she has turned down two internal requests by simply not replying.

Nandita Basu — Head of Design, Lisbon. Wants teams organised around the supervisor's shift, not the software's layers; has documented eleven ways the system tells an operator a part has failed. Not saying: she is down to four designers from six and expects to lose one more in November.

Shalini Menon — Director, Customer Success APAC, Kuala Lumpur. The only person who has visited all nineteen Dhaatu plants. Believes the problem is not structure but that nobody tells customers no. Incentive: her renewal number includes the ₹11.4 crore.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is today's structure, including the pod that exists because of a contract rather than a design.

The Darpan agreement runs to 31 March 2027 with 18,000 units of offtake and a ₹4.6 crore penalty; Jaanch is tracking to 15,400. The Coimbatore site's state industrial-promotion benefit is tied to jobs maintained there. Tamil Nadu plants shut for Ayudha Puja in late October and the Diwali freeze closes customer sites from 4 November; whatever is announced has eleven usable weeks before the year's final quarter.

  4. Clause 7.4 promises a dedicated pod to one customer. Is that an organisational design question, a contracting question, or a sales-discipline question — and who at Jaanch should own it?

What do you put on it, what do you deliberately leave off, and what do you tell the board on the 9th about what you do not yet know — particularly if you believe Exhibit 6's footnote matters more than the chart above it?

She had not known that file existed. Outside, the last second-shift bus turned onto Avinashi Road, carrying operators who would stand in front of her company's cameras again at six in the morning, in plants where, whichever chart she chose, nothing would change for months.

Product Org Models: Cutting the System Before Cutting the Chart

Outcome, component, segment, platform — four ways to draw the boundary of a product team. The choice looks like an organisational preference. It is in fact a claim about where a system's dependencies actually lie, and it can be tested with data the company already has.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On 4 March 2026, Nandita Rau, Chief Product Officer of Parikrama Payments Network, opened two quarters of merge data in the firm's Lower Parel office. Parikrama, founded in 2017 by two former NPCI engineers, processed card and UPI payments for 41,000 merchants at roughly ₹640 crore of annualised revenue, on 310 engineers and 38 PMs in twenty-two teams. One number had brought her there: authorisation success rate — the share of attempted card payments that completed — stood at 84.6% against the best Indian gateway's 91.2%. Each point was worth ₹6.1 crore a year, so the gap was worth ₹40 crore. Her CEO wanted a reorganisation into three merchant segments: Enterprise, Growth and the new Platform Partners business. Nandita suspected that cut would make authorisation worse, and had until the 28 March board to say so with evidence.

Three weeks later, Karan Bhatnagar, VP Product at Pratibimb Vision Systems in Pune, faced the same question in a different shape. Pratibimb sold AI visual inspection to automotive plants: a camera and lighting rig, an edge inference box, a cloud training service and a plant-floor dashboard, on 210 lines across 46 plants in Pune, Chennai, Sanand and Hosur. At a Chennai transmission-parts plant the false-reject rate — good parts flagged as defective and re-inspected by hand — was 3.8% against a contractual ceiling of 1.5%, worth ₹45 lakh of penalty a quarter. His 128 engineers sat in eight component teams. An advisor said the answer was obvious: a False-Reject team with end-to-end ownership. Karan's hesitation was not political. His cameras shipped on a nine-month cycle, his models retrained fortnightly, his dashboard weekly. One team cannot hold three clocks that differ by a factor of thirty-nine.

2. What a product org model is, and the argument it inherited

A product org model is the rule by which a company decides what each team owns and is accountable for moving. Four rules recur. An outcome team owns a measurable result — authorisation success, false-reject rate — with authority over whatever must change to move it. A component team owns a part of the technical system, whichever outcomes depend on it. A segment team owns a class of customers and serves them the whole product. A platform team owns a shared capability built once so others need not build it five times. Real organisations mix these; the question is which is primary, because the primary cut determines what can be decided without a meeting.

The argument predates product management. Alfred Chandler's Strategy and Structure (1962) showed the multidivisional form emerging at DuPont and General Motors because functional structures could not cope with product diversity. Lawrence and Lorsch (1967) established that organisations must both differentiate and integrate, and that integration cost rises with differentiation. In the same year Melvin Conway observed that any organisation designing a system produces a design mirroring its own communication structure, and Jay Galbraith (1973) recast org design as information processing: a structure reduces the decisions that must cross a boundary. Modern practice added evidence: MacCormack, Rusnak and Baldwin's 2012 study of paired codebases found products built by distributed organisations measurably more modular than equivalent co-located ones.

Three schools disagree in ways that matter at a whiteboard. The outcome-and-empowerment school — Amazon's two-pizza doctrine, Marty Cagan's EMPOWERED (2020), and Skelton and Pais's Team Topologies (2019), which names stream-aligned, platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem types and defaults to the first — signs that a team should own a problem end to end and be measured on the result. It will not sign the claim that every capability deserves a team.

The functional-excellence school, most visibly Apple as described by Joel Podolny and Morten Hansen in Harvard Business Review (2020), signs the opposite: depth of expertise concentrated under expert leaders beats distributed accountability, and the coordination cost is worth paying. It regards team-level outcome ownership as a way of guaranteeing nobody is world-class at anything. The market-facing school, descending from Sloan and from Bartlett and Ghoshal, signs: where customer classes require genuinely different product decisions, the segment is the correct primary cut. That is Parikrama's CEO's school.

Fig. 1 — Every product organisation is a partition of the same grid: outcomes across the top, subsystems down the side. A column is an outcome team, a row a component or platform team, and a segment cut replicates the grid.

3. Mechanics: cut the system before you cut the chart

Competent practitioners choose an axis and argue about it. Experts first measure where the dependencies are, because the cheapest cut severs the fewest. The apparatus is the design structure matrix, elaborated by Eppinger and Browning: record which subsystems each merged change touched, build a co-change matrix, cluster. Nandita ran this over 612 changes from the previous two quarters.

Fig. 2 — Two clusters fall out unambiguously: checkout, routing and tokenisation co-change at 33–41%, ledger and reporting at 46%. Every cross-cluster pair sits at 14% or below.

The matrix answered the CEO's proposal without any argument about philosophy. A segment cut would place Enterprise, Growth and Platform Partners teams each astride the whole authorisation cluster, so three subsystems that co-change a third of the time would be owned three ways. The clusters instead named the outcomes: authorisation, money movement, onboarding. This is the step usually left implicit — outcomes are discovered from the dependency structure, not chosen from a strategy deck.

The second implicit step decides whether the reorganisation delivers speed, because not all shared work can be absorbed. Parikrama's tokenisation vault is mandated by the Reserve Bank's card-on-file regime; it is audited, it holds the keys, and forking it creates three compliance surfaces. It stays a component team. Given an irreducible shared dependency, how much speed can a reorganisation buy? The answer has the shape of Amdahl's Law: if a fraction f of a team's work still routes through shared components and autonomy speeds the rest by a factor k, the overall speed-up is 1 ÷ [ f + (1−f)/k ].

Two conclusions follow, both counter-intuitive to executives expecting linear returns. The ceiling is set by f: even perfect autonomy on the rest caps Parikrama near 2.9×. And cutting f from 0.35 to 0.15 beats tripling the autonomy multiplier — while f falls not by redrawing boxes but by investing in the shared team's capacity.

Hence the third step, which almost nobody performs: treat the shared team as a queue. Nandita measured the vault team — seven engineers, a typical request taking four working days of service, arriving at 19 a month against a capacity of 22. Utilisation was 0.86. Expected wait scales roughly as ρ/(1−ρ) times service time: 0.86 / 0.14 × 4 = 24.6 days of waiting for four days of work. Reinertsen made this the centre of The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009): queue length, not team shape, is where development time hides.

Fig. 3 — The curve is convex, which is the point: between ρ=0.5 and 0.7 the penalty is mild, past 0.85 it explodes. Two more engineers moved the vault to ρ=0.68 and cut expected wait from 24.6 days to 8.5.

Nandita's proposal therefore had three parts in a deliberate order: fund the shared component below 0.7 utilisation; publish an interface contract so most requests become self-service; only then cut the outcome teams. Reorganising first would hand autonomous teams a queue that ate the autonomy.

4. When the outcome default holds, and when it misleads

The Team Topologies default — prefer stream-aligned teams — rests on four conditions statable as testable claims.

One: the outcome's subsystems form a cluster. Parikrama passes; its authorisation cluster is dense. Pratibimb fails: false-reject rate is driven by optics, firmware, model thresholds and operator workflow, which almost never co-change.

Two: the team can hold the cognitive load. Skelton and Pais give a crude but usable rule of two or three domains per team. Parikrama's authorisation team holds two and a half; Pratibimb's would hold four, two of which need engineers who cannot be hired interchangeably.

Three: cadences inside the boundary are within an order of magnitude. Parikrama's subsystems deploy weekly or faster; Pratibimb's span one week to thirty-nine. When cadences diverge that far, the boundary becomes a permanent negotiation and fast work is dragged to the pace of slow.

Four: the outcome is attributable. Authorisation success qualifies because issuer-side declines can be separated from gateway-side failures in the logs. Where a metric cannot be decomposed, ownership is theatre, and the honest move is to own a leading indicator that can.

The idea is actively misleading in two situations. First, when a company has a competence problem rather than a coordination problem: reorganising a team without a strong technical lead gives the same people a new name and a metric they still cannot move. Second, below roughly thirty engineers, Conway's Law has nothing to bite on.

5. Hard edges: two-sided, regulated, hardware and AI-native

Marketplaces carry an axis the four models do not name: supply and demand are different customers with different products but one matching economy. Flipkart, Swiggy and Uber all converge on separate supply and demand organisations plus a shared matching and pricing platform — and all find the same seam, since pricing, incentives and ranking sit between the sides, and whoever owns them sets both sides' strategy. Mature handling makes the seam a platform team with a published objective function and a forum in which both sides argue its parameters. Such companies call pricing neutral infrastructure; in fact it is where the strategy fight is held.

Regulated products introduce components that cannot be dissolved however inconvenient: Parikrama's vault, a bank's core ledger, an insurer's rating engine. Each has a named accountable owner in the regulatory sense, and distributing it multiplies audit surface rather than sharing ownership. Expert practice accepts a few non-negotiable component teams, resources them generously, and forces the rest of the coupling into explicit interfaces.

Hardware-plus-software organisations face Pratibimb's problem: the cut must respect the slowest clock. The mature answer is to organise by cadence band and reconnect the bands with a named outcome owner who holds no direct reports but does hold the metric, the forum and the escalation path. Ola Electric, Bosch's plant-automation businesses and Apple all run versions of this, differing in how much authority that role carries.

AI-native products add a genuinely new seam. Model, evaluation harness, data pipeline and product surface can be owned separately, but a model change with no product change can alter user-visible behaviour overnight, which makes the harness a shared component with power to block. Several large AI firms now treat evals as a platform team with authority over release gates: functionally a component team with a veto, which the empowerment school dislikes and the field has not resolved.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

The axis you publish is rarely the axis you run

Every organisation has a declared model and a real one, and the tell is where an urgent escalation travels at 11 p.m. If a settlement outage routes to a director who convenes four leads himself, he is the real unit of ownership. Charts describe reporting, not coordination.

Conway's Law is about communication, not reporting lines

Two teams under different VPs who share a channel, review each other's code and share an on-call rotation are, for Conway's purposes, one team; two under one VP who communicate by ticket are two. The tell is the medium of the average cross-team interaction, so the cheapest org change is often a change to who sits in which review.

At high utilisation the chart is a second-order lever

The queueing curve is convex, so a shared team above 0.85 utilisation swamps every structural effect. The tell is variance: when the same request takes four days one month and five weeks the next, you are watching a queue. Dependent teams are not being deprioritised; they are arriving at a saturated server.

Cadence beats outcome as a cut where clocks diverge

When release cycles inside a boundary differ by more than an order of magnitude, the boundary will not hold. The tell is a team keeping two roadmaps in different units, one in sprints and one in model years. The obvious answer — make the slow part faster — ignores physical floors in validation and tooling.

A segment cut bets on differences in decisions, not revenue

Segments earn teams when they force different product choices, not different sales motions or price points. The diagnostic is blunt: name three things the Enterprise team shipped that the Growth team would have refused. If the answer is none, a go-to-market structure has been built into engineering.

Platform teams should be measured on adoption without mandate

Amazon's widely recounted 2002 service-interface mandate is cited as proof that platforms may compel adoption; the internal-product school argues that a platform its consumers would not choose is a tax. The tell is a memo requiring use. Regulated components need one, but a mandate issued to fix low adoption buries the evidence of a bad interface.

Reorganisation cost is relationship re-formation, not learning

People relearn a codebase in weeks and rebuild trust across boundaries in quarters. The tell is escalation volume to directors, which spikes after any reorganisation and, in healthy cases, returns to baseline within two quarters. If it does not, the new boundaries cut through work that must be co-decided.

Hybrids are normal; unacknowledged hybrids are dangerous

Almost every organisation past 150 engineers mixes axes. The failure is not the mixing but the refusal to say which is primary, because that pushes conflict upward without a rule. The tell is a decision reaching an executive with two competent, mutually exclusive recommendations and no principle for choosing between them.

7. How this differs by product type and by stage

Consumer products with one large homogeneous audience have no defensible segment cut, so the real argument is outcome versus component, and outcome nearly always wins because consumer metrics decompose cleanly and deployment is continuous. B2B and enterprise differ in one real respect: buying-committee complexity means some capabilities — provisioning, audit, data residency — are demanded by one segment and unwanted by others, which supports a thin segment layer above an outcome layer. Marketplaces differ because the two sides have separate economics and a contested seam; hardware differs because of cadence, irreversibility and component lead times, a first-order difference rather than a nuance; AI products differ mainly in the evaluation seam.

Where the difference is not real is worth saying plainly. Whether to run four outcome teams or five, what teams are called, and whether design reports into product or into a design function are not determined by product type; organisations debating them as strategy are avoiding the dependency question. Stage matters, non-linearly. Below thirty engineers there is no org model worth having. Between thirty and eighty, hand-off delay becomes visible and a first cut is needed. Between eighty and three hundred, platform teams become justified as duplication cost overtakes coordination cost. Above three hundred every organisation is a hybrid, and the question shifts to the quality of interfaces and forums between structures.

8. Three worked examples

Parikrama: a success with an honest caveat. Nandita took the vault team from seven engineers to nine in April 2026, published an interface contract in May, and cut three outcome teams — Authorisation, Money Movement, Onboarding — in June, keeping the vault and a small compliance team. Over three quarters authorisation success rose from 84.6% to 88.9%, worth ₹26.2 crore annualised at ₹6.1 crore a point. The caveat: throughput fell about 22% for one quarter. At 310 engineers and ₹42 lakh fully loaded each, a quarter costs ₹32.5 crore, so the dip cost some ₹7.2 crore. It paid back inside four months — but a company reorganising annually would never clear the dip.

Pratibimb: a cadence cut rather than an outcome cut. Karan decomposed the 3.8% false-reject rate: 2.4 points from model thresholds, 1.1 from lighting and lens geometry, 0.3 from operator workflow. He organised into three cadence bands — Sensing (optics, firmware, edge runtime; nine-month clock), Model (data, training, evaluation; fortnightly) and Factory Experience (dashboard, alerts, workflow; weekly) — and appointed a principal PM as named owner of false-reject rate, with no direct reports, a monthly review and the right to call a stop-ship. Within five months Chennai fell to 2.1%, cutting quarterly penalty exposure from ₹45 lakh to ₹12 lakh. The residual 0.6 points were optics-driven and waited on the hardware clock; an outcome team would not have made the lenses arrive sooner.

Pahchaan Identity Systems: a failure and its recovery. Pahchaan, a Gurugram video-KYC vendor serving NBFCs, moved in 2024 from fourteen component teams to six outcome teams in a single announcement, with no dependency inventory and no platform layer. Within two quarters four of the six had built their own document-OCR wrapper. On the same test set their accuracies were 94.1%, 91.7%, 88.9% and 95.2%, so one PAN card could pass one onboarding flow and fail another — which an audit recorded as an inconsistent-controls finding. The recovery was not a reorganisation back: leadership re-formed a single OCR component team with a mandated interface and a six-week migration window per consumer, and tracked distinct OCR code paths in production from four to one over five months. Rework ran ₹3.2 crore and the roadmap cost eleven months. Outcome teams were not wrong for Pahchaan; the sequence was.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether outcome ownership beats functional depth at scale. The functional school's strongest evidence is Apple: the most valuable product company in history runs functionally, without product P&Ls, and its differentiation rests on component excellence — silicon, camera, display — that no outcome team would have funded so deeply. The outcome school's evidence is Amazon and the wide class of software businesses where speed of learning dominates depth in any one component. For the functional position to be wrong, Apple's success would have to be despite its structure, its integration cost paid invisibly by an unusual executive team. For the outcome position to be wrong, deep-moat products would have to lose only where the moat was shallow.

Whether the Spotify model was ever a model. The 2012 squads-and-tribes paper became the most copied structure in product management. Jeremiah Lee, who worked there, argued in 2020 that Spotify never ran it as described and that copies reliably produced ambiguity about who decided what. The steelman for copying is that the principles — small durable teams, aligned autonomy, chapters for craft — hold independently of Spotify. The steelman against is that a snapshot of an unusual company was consumed as a template, and templates transfer structure without conditions.

Whether platform teams may mandate. The internal-product school holds that mandates mask bad interfaces and adoption must be earned. The counter-position holds that in regulated or correctness-critical domains optionality is itself the defect — Pahchaan's four OCR implementations are the argument. Both are right in their domains, and nobody has a rule for the boundary.

Whether org model matters at all. The most uncomfortable position, held quietly by many experienced executives, is that structure explains far less performance variance than leadership quality and strategic clarity, and that reorganisations often substitute for deciding what the product should be. No company runs the counterfactual, so there is no clean evidence either way.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this arrives at an org discussion with four models and an opinion about which is best. Someone who has internalised it arrives with three artefacts: a co-change matrix, a list of dependencies that cannot be dissolved and why, and a utilisation figure for every shared team. They argue about sequence rather than shape, because the platform must precede the autonomy, and they can say which axis is primary and what rule resolves conflicts with the secondary one. And they treat reorganisation as an expensive instrument with a known transition cost, used when the data says the cut is wrong — not when the metric is disappointing and something visible must be done.

12. What Nandita and Karan decided

Nandita presented the co-change matrix on 28 March and argued that the proposed segment cut would slice the authorisation cluster three ways at exactly the moment the company needed it to move as one. The board approved an outcome primary cut with a thin Enterprise segment layer owning contract-specific work only and — the part she insisted on — funded the vault before any team moved. She stated the conflict rule explicitly: where the segment layer and an outcome team disagree, the outcome team decides and the segment layer escalates with evidence.

Karan declined the advice to build a false-reject team. He cut by cadence, named an owner for the outcome rather than a team, and accepted that part of the problem would move on a nine-month clock. His reasoning, in a memo of 24 March: the cut minimising coordination cost severs the fewest tight couplings, and at Pratibimb those couplings ran along clocks rather than customer journeys.

Discussion questions

  1. Nandita's argument rested on six months of merge data. When would that evidence mislead her?
  2. Karan gave an individual the outcome and teams the cadences. What does that require of him that a team-based structure would not, and how would you know within two quarters that it had failed?
  3. Pahchaan's recovery mandated a single OCR interface. Was that a correction of the reorganisation or a partial reversal, and what evidence a year later would distinguish the two?

13. Going deeper

Empowered teams vs feature teams is the prerequisite argument: the org model decides whether empowerment is structurally available at all. Team topologies and ownership boundaries formalises the four team types and three interaction modes, giving language for the interfaces this page treats as given. Product operations staffs the forums and data that hold a hybrid together. AI-era product operating model takes up the evaluation seam. Scaling the product organisation with the product develops the stage thresholds of section seven, and global platform, local product tension applies the segment cut across geographies. Managing product managers and hiring PMs decide whether a team can exercise the authority a chart grants it; PM levels and career ladders matter because an outcome cut demands more senior judgement per team. Product reviews and decision forums are where a hybrid's conflicts are resolved or left to fester, cross-functional rituals carry the coordination no structure eliminates, and product culture decides whether a conflict rule is obeyed when inconvenient.

Where Influence Comes From: The PM at a Startup and at a Large Company

Two product leaders, one week in September 2026, and one question under both their problems: what is the cheapest defensible way to get a decision made here?

1. Two decisions, one week

On Monday, 14 September 2026, Meher Bhatnagar took a call in a hangar outside Pune. Antariksh Drone Systems, where she had been VP of product for five months, built spray drones and the software that flew them: seventy-four people, ₹31 crore of a Series B unspent. An agronomist at a sugarcane co-operative in Belagavi was telling her that Antariksh's drones had sprayed at 2.4 metres where the crop stage wanted 3.1, scorching eleven acres. Her team had a firmware change ready that would key spray height to a crop-stage field the app already collected. Shipping it required nobody's permission but her own. That was precisely the difficulty.

On Wednesday, 1,180 kilometres away in Mumbai, Devdatt Iyengar opened a document he had been circulating for nineteen days. Devdatt was group product head for collections at Chandrabhaga Financial Corporation, a listed lender and insurer with 26,400 employees and 2.6 crore borrowers. His proposal was narrow: move the first missed-payment reminder from a Day-3 message naming the penalty to a Day-1 message naming the amount, with a one-tap payment link. A holdout test on 40,000 accounts had lifted Day-15 recovery from 61.2% to 67.4%. Seven names sat on the slip; four had not opened the document.

Both were competent, and each was stuck in the shape the other would have found trivial. Meher could ship in an afternoon and feared what that would cost if the logic was wrong in a way her three-person hardware team had not imagined; with no committee to hide behind, she had nobody to catch her either. Devdatt had five functions who would catch any error, and their attention was so rationed that nineteen days produced four unopened tabs. The naive reading is that Meher has too little process and Devdatt too much. The argument here is that both are mispricing the same thing.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define influence precisely, since loose use of the word causes most of the confusion: it is a product manager's capacity to cause a decision to be made and a resource committed without formal authority over the people or the budget. It is a stock, not a trait, and its exchange rate is set by the organisation, not the PM.

At an early-stage company the dominant deposit is resolved ambiguity — a call under real uncertainty that turns out defensible. At a large company it is delivered alignment — a commitment obtained from people who each held a partial veto, then honoured. Why should the currency differ at all?

The intellectual history answers that. Larry Greiner's 1972 Harvard Business Review essay on evolution and revolution in growing organisations established that management problems change predictably with size and age. The mechanism came two decades later, from Michael Jensen and William Meckling on specific knowledge and the organisation of decision rights: decision rights migrate toward whoever holds knowledge that cannot be cheaply transmitted upward, and the counterweight is agency cost, the expected loss from a decision made by someone whose incentives are imperfectly aligned with the firm's. Push the decision to the knowledge and you buy speed with exposure; pull it to the centre and you buy control with delay. The problem belongs to the economics of who may say yes, which lets the schools be stated as propositions they would sign.

These are not five views of one elephant. The decision-rights and personal-credibility schools give Devdatt opposite advice: one says the seven-name slip is the disease, the other that it is furniture and he should buy coffee for the four who have not opened the tab.

3. Mechanics: pricing the alignment tax

Experts, however they phrase it, price each decision before routing it. Four inputs: the blast radius of being wrong, in rupees of remediation plus regulatory and reputational exposure; the team's prior defect rate on that class of decision; the marginal catch rate of one more independent reviewer; and the carrying cost of delay.

Write expected error cost with k reviewers as C × p0 × rk, where C is blast radius, p0 the unreviewed probability of a material defect, and r the residual fraction a reviewer leaves behind. The k-th reviewer earns its place when the error cost it removes exceeds its delay. Take r = 0.6: each competent independent reviewer catches about forty per cent of what survived the last one, roughly what inspection literature reports.

The second removes ₹8.4 lakh: still worth it. The third removes ₹5.04 lakh against ₹5.7 lakh, and is not. Meher's answer on Monday is two independent reviewers — chief engineer Vikrant Joag and an outside agronomist — in six days rather than an afternoon. Her instinct that she should not ship alone was right; her assumption that the alternative was a committee was not.

Three second-order effects follow, and this is where the expertise sits. First, the optimum is a property of the decision, not the company; any organisation with one review depth for all decisions is wrong on most of them, over-reviewing the cheap and under-reviewing the expensive — large firms characteristically err the first way, startups the second. Second, k* rises endogenously as a company grows, because C rises with users and revenue while r stays put; a founder complaining the company "got slow" is often watching correct repricing and calling it decay. Third, the delay term contains runway at a startup, so its discount rate is genuinely higher — which is why a lower k* there is legitimate rather than cultural.

4. When the distinction holds, and when it misleads

Claim one: blast radius, not headcount, sets the alignment tax. Test it by comparing review depth across two products of similar size in one firm. It holds at Chandrabhaga, where the dashboard row shows depth detached from exposure — evidence against the firm's process, not the claim. At Antariksh it holds so strongly that seventy-four people need two reviewers on flight logic, which is why "startups move fast" misleads Meher.

Claim two: at a startup the binding constraint is the availability of a decision-maker; at a large company it is the availability of attention. Devdatt's nineteen days contained perhaps six hours of review; the rest was queue. Meher's afternoon contained no queue and no review. Claim three: an influence stock is spent, not displayed — test it by asking what the PM stopped doing to get the last decision through.

The distinction actively misleads in three situations. A startup regulated from birth — a twelve-month-old lender under Reserve Bank of India fair-practices obligations — has bank-sized C on day one, and the startup playbook is a route to an enforcement letter. A separated new-venture unit gives its PMs startup economics on a bigco payroll. And when a startup is slow because of ownership boundaries rather than stage, "we need less process" is precisely wrong: that case belongs to the organisation-design school.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

The interesting failures cluster at seams, where two parts of one company correctly run different values of k and neither has said so. Hardware plus software. Antariksh has two clock speeds: firmware tied to airframes already in fields, and an app that ships twice a week. The expert move is not to slow the app but to make the seam explicit: the app may change anything that does not alter a flight parameter, and anything that does inherits firmware's k of two. Meher's change crosses that line, so it was never an app decision.

Two-sided marketplaces. At Aavaran Commerce Exchange, a 910-person apparel marketplace in Gurugram, Nandita Sur owns buyer discovery and another PM owns seller tooling. A ranking change lifting buyer conversion 3% suppresses the top decile of sellers by 11% of impressions. Neither PM's blast radius contains the other's users, so both compute an honest k too low for the firm. Mature marketplaces answer with one liquidity owner holding a standing veto on ranking — a named reviewer, not a forum.

Regulated and multi-product. Chandrabhaga's lending and insurance businesses share a customer app. A change to the notification tray is low-C for lending and high-C for insurance, where a mis-timed nudge can constitute mis-selling; the slip cannot be a property of the surface. Large firms say they maintain a RACI. What they keep is an informal register of changes that have caused trouble, held in three or four long-tenured heads — which works, is undocumented, and leaves when those people do.

AI-native products. At Anuvaad Speech Systems, thirty-eight people in Hyderabad building speech models for call-centre quality scoring, r itself collapses: a human reading a prompt change cannot form a reliable prior about its effect on a distribution of outputs, so the review is real but the forty per cent is fiction. The competent response moves the reviewer from judgement to evidence — a name on a slip replaced by an eval suite of 1,800 labelled calls that must clear a threshold before release. Influence there accrues to whoever owns that suite: influence following decision rights rather than title.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

Influence is a stock with a readable balance. The tell is not how often a PM is consulted but whether decisions in their area happen without them and then get reversed. A PM whose absence changes nothing has a balance of zero, however full their calendar. The obvious reading inverts the truth: at scale, being in every room is what a PM does when they cannot trust a decision to go correctly without them.

The ratchet. Review steps are added after incidents and essentially never removed, so depth drifts monotonically above k*. The expert's diagnostic is one question: when was a step last deleted? An organisation that cannot name an instance has a ratchet, and its depth reflects its worst historical week rather than its present risk.

Surprise, not disagreement, destroys influence at scale. Devdatt can survive a stakeholder who thinks he is wrong; he cannot survive one who learns of his change from their own boss. The tell is who learned first, and in what order. Hence something counter-intuitive: pre-reads protect standing rather than transmit information, which is why sending one to everybody at once is worse than sending it first to the most exposed person.

Founder proximity is real currency that depreciates. Below forty people it dominates everything; by two hundred it is a liability, because corridor decisions cannot be audited and those outside the corridor stop trying. The tell is whether a written decision log exists at all — companies that survive the transition acquire one within a quarter of crossing a hundred people, because the corridor stops scaling.

"Ownership" is routinely conflated with holding a decision right. Ask a PM who owns a surface, then who can veto a change and whose veto is final. Where the answers diverge, the PM holds accountability without authority — a structural condition, not a personal failing.

Startup speed is often borrowed from a future audit. Every "we will document it later" is a liability entered without a due date; the diagnostic is whether anyone can reconstruct why a shipped decision was made. Antariksh's 2.4-metre default was set in a corridor in March by someone who has since left — the real root cause of the eleven scorched acres.

Attention, not approval, is the scarce good at scale. Devdatt's four unopened tabs are not resistance. The diagnostic: how many approvals arrive within twenty-four hours of a direct personal nudge? If most do, the problem was queueing and the fix is sequencing. If few do, his change is low on other people's lists, and the fix is to attach it to something high on theirs.

A high k is not a slow organisation, and both settings punish one error. Five reviewers in parallel with a twenty-four-hour service level beat two in series with no deadline, so experts attack the scheduling of review before its depth — depth usually has a defender and scheduling almost never does. Underneath, the ex-bigco joiner convening six calendars in week two and the ex-startup joiner shipping without sign-off make one mistake in two dialects: drawing on a balance they have not built.

7. How this differs across product types and stages

Some of the variation claimed here is real. It is real for consumer products, where blast radius is set by audience size and press exposure rather than contract, so C jumps discontinuously at scale. It is real for enterprise B2B, where a startup inherits its customers' governance from the first design partner and has its k set outside the building. It is real for hardware, where irreversibility rather than exposure drives the sum: no one rolls back an airframe. It is decoration for internal tooling. And it is overstated for AI products, which need not more governance but differently evidenced governance.

8. Three worked examples

Antariksh, and the value of two reviewers. Meher took the six-day route. Vikrant modelled spray drift at four crop stages; the agronomist caught what he had not — 9% of plots had no crop-stage entry and would fall back to the old default. The fix was a hard block rather than a fallback. Shipped on Monday, the change would have been right for the 91% and silently unchanged for the plots most likely to be misflown. Cost of delay: about ₹11 lakh; expected loss avoided, roughly ₹22 lakh.

Chandrabhaga, and the sequencing fix. Devdatt stopped circulating and sequenced instead, taking the change to chief risk officer Farida Merchant alone, with the holdout numbers and a one-page note on what the message did not say. Her assent turned the remaining reviewers' question from "is this safe?" into "risk has cleared this; do I object?" Elapsed time to full sign-off: five business days, against nineteen already spent. He also dropped two reviewers by arguing their catch rate on message copy was indistinguishable from zero. Annualised value of the lift: about ₹41 crore of earlier collections — which is why ₹24 lakh per reviewer understated the delay cost, and why he should have run the arithmetic on day one.

Chaturang Grocery Cloud, and the failure. Chaturang, a Chennai grocery-logistics platform, grew from 90 to 620 people in twenty-two months. Its product head, Sameer Khandekar, kept the startup playbook: decisions by whoever was closest to the problem, no routing slips. The company had nine incidents serious enough for a post-mortem, and after each one a reviewer joined an informal list nobody had designed and nobody pruned. Median approvers went 2 to 7, latency 6 to 31 days, shipped changes per quarter 34 to 11. The failure was not adding process — rising C justified some — but adding it by accretion rather than by pricing, so depth tracked the memory of incidents instead of present exposure. Recovery took two quarters: price every recurring decision type, set an explicit k and a named owner, and delete in writing every reviewer that number did not justify. Approvers fell to 3, latency to 11 days, throughput to 27, with no new tooling.

The second row's cost is social rather than technical: when a PM ships past a reviewer and is caught, the organisation adds a step for everybody. Individual speed bought at the cost of the collective k is the most expensive trade a PM at scale can make.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is the large firm's alignment cost value-protecting or rent-protecting? The efficiency position, steelmanned: review depth at regulated scale is a rational response to blast radius, and post-mortems of large-firm incidents almost always find that the step which would have caught the problem existed and was skipped; its evidence is that unreviewed decisions at scale fail rarely and catastrophically. The rent-seeking position, steelmanned: review rights are the principal currency of internal status, so functions acquire them for reasons unconnected to risk, and the signature is that depth never falls when exposure falls. The first position would be wrong if removing reviewers in a controlled way did not raise incident rates — which Chaturang weakly supports and one case cannot settle.

Does influence transfer across stages? The personal-credibility position: influence travels with the person, and stalled transitions reflect unwillingness to do the relational work; its evidence is the minority who move both directions successfully within two quarters. The structural position: the currency genuinely differs, and transfer failures cluster too tightly by direction to be individual effort. Each would be wrong if outcomes were better explained by the other's variable, and nobody has the dataset.

Build process ahead of the pain, or wait for it? The anticipatory view holds that decision-class pricing at 120 people costs a week and saves Chaturang's twenty-two months. The reactive view holds that pre-built process is calibrated to an imagined blast radius, that imagined radii run too large, and that governance installed before the incidents is the wrong governance, permanently. Both sides accept the ratchet; they disagree about whether its first click is better placed by foresight or evidence.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this talks about startups and large companies. Someone who has internalised it talks about decisions, one at a time, and can say within a minute what a decision is worth being wrong about — then routes by that number rather than by policy. They can name the two or three decision classes where their organisation's review depth is wrong, and its direction. They treat influence as a balance to spend, and can say what the last withdrawal bought. Arriving somewhere new, they spend a fortnight learning whose no is final before proposing anything.

12. What Meher and Devdatt decided

Meher did not ship on Monday. She wrote down, for the first time at Antariksh, the eleven recurring decision classes her team touched, priced each in rupees, and set a review depth against it: zero for copy and onboarding, one for pricing and navigation, two for anything that changed a flight parameter. The spray-height change went out the following Monday with a hard block on missing crop-stage data. She then did the thing that mattered more — gave the list to her CEO, Suhasini Rane, and asked her to approve it once, so neither would have to approve individual decisions again. The scarce good at Antariksh was not permission but founder attention, and a one-time schedule bought back more of it than individual asks ever would.

Devdatt shipped in five days after nineteen, having sequenced Farida Merchant first and dropped two reviewers on the arithmetic. He also proposed something he expected to lose: changes below ₹50 lakh of exposure would carry two reviewers on a forty-eight-hour service level, and only those above ₹5 crore the full slip. He lost, for now; the functions that would have surrendered review rights argued, not unreasonably, that exposure is easier to assert than to measure. He intends to return with the collections numbers attached.

Discussion questions

  1. Meher's list makes her review depth explicit and auditable. What does she lose by writing it down, and when would Antariksh have been better off leaving that judgement in her head?
  2. Devdatt's opponents claim exposure is easier to assert than measure. Is that an argument for uniform review depth, or about who may set the number? Which school in section 2 does each reading commit you to?
  3. Chaturang recovered throughput without new tooling and without an incident in the two quarters after. How much should that update your view of the efficiency position, and what observation within six months would change your answer?
