PM at a Startup vs a Large Company

Where does a product manager's influence actually come from — and why does the same person who moves mountains in one setting struggle to move a meeting in the other?

1. A Thursday in Bengaluru

On the second Thursday of September 2026, Rohan Kapadia sat in a glass-walled room at Ishan Mobility Cloud, a sixty-person fleet-safety startup, staring at a calendar invite he had just sent to six people. He had done this a hundred times before, in six years as a senior product manager at Indraprastha Retail Group, a forty-thousand-employee retail conglomerate, where a feature this size — a fatigue-alert system pinging a driver's cab when steering patterns suggested drowsiness — would have gone through Store Operations, IT Security, Legal, Finance and a monthly Central Product Council before one line of code shipped. That was simply how Indraprastha worked, and Rohan had become good at it.

He had been at Ishan for eleven days, nine of them spent trying to get six people — the CEO, two co-founders, the head of fleet operations, the lone data scientist, and a safety consultant — into one room. Two cancelled; one joined late from Nashik with no signal. That same morning, rival startup Ghoomti Mobility Systems announced a near-identical feature, and Ishan had roughly fourteen months of runway left. Rohan's invite was, without his noticing, an attempt to import a bigco decision process into a company that could not afford the fifteen minutes it cost, let alone the fifteen days.

2. The idea: where influence comes from

A product manager's influence — the capacity to get a decision made and a resource committed without owning the people or the budget — is never free-floating; it is drawn from a specific source, and that source changes with the shape of the organisation. At an early-stage company, influence is drawn from resolved ambiguity: the PM who can look at an undefined situation, make a defensible call, and be right often enough earns the right to keep making calls. At a large, established company, influence is drawn from built alignment: the PM who can get a defined set of stakeholders — each holding real veto power over a piece of the outcome — to agree, earns the right to move the organisation's machinery.

The distinction has no single named inventor, but its roots run through Larry Greiner's 1972 Harvard Business Review article "Evolution and Revolution as Organizations Grow," which argued that management problems change predictably with an organisation's size and age. Practitioner writers translated that into product-specific language over the following decades — Ben Horowitz's essays on scaling teams, later Marty Cagan's operating-model writing — making explicit what Greiner had implied: the skills that make someone effective do not transfer automatically across stages, because the currency of influence changes underneath them.

"At a startup, my influence is a function of how much ambiguity I can resolve myself. At a large company, it's a function of how many people I can get to agree before I move."

That is the sentence Rohan needed, and did not yet have, on his ninth day.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics are the same five steps in both settings; what differs is which step dominates the PM's time.

Step one — map where the decision right sits. At a startup this is usually a person: the founder, or whoever they have quietly delegated the call to. At a bigco it is usually a body: a council or a named approver in a RACI chart the PM must go find.

Step two — diagnose the scarce resource. At a startup it is cash runway, and therefore time; every unshipped week is a week closer to the end of the money. At a bigco it is coordination bandwidth — dozens of initiatives competing for the same people's attention in the same recurring meetings.

Step three — choose the currency you spend. At a startup it is founder trust and shipped outcomes: each proven-right call earns more delegation; each wrong one spends it down fast. At a bigco it is alignment capital: relationships maintained, pre-reads sent ahead of meetings, nobody ever surprised in front of their boss.

Step four — build the artifact that currency buys. At a startup, a working prototype or a pilot with real numbers. At a bigco, a document — a PRD with named sign-offs — giving people who will never share a room an identical, defensible record of what they agreed to.

Step five — close the loop. Startups skip this by moving to the next fire without saying what was decided; bigcos skip it by treating sign-off as the finish line rather than confirming what shipped is what was approved.

Fig. 1 — The loop is structurally identical on both sides; what changes is who holds "go" and what evidence they require.

4. A worked example, with the arithmetic shown

At Indraprastha, Rohan's fatigue-alert equivalent had been a "buy online, pick up in store" rollout across 220 outlets. Five reviews stood between concept and launch: Store Operations (15 business days), IT Security (15), Legal (10), Finance (5), and a Central Product Council meeting the first Monday of each month, requiring a completed deck ten days beforehand. Run in parallel, the longest review — 15 days — set the pace, but if that mark fell after the month's cutoff, the request waited roughly 20 more days for the next Council: 15 + 20 = 35 days. One review in three came back "revise and resubmit," adding 10 more days on average — a typical total of about 45 business days, nine calendar weeks, before a customer saw the feature.

At Ishan, the decision sat with three people: Rohan, CEO Priya Subramaniam, and head of fleet operations Aman Dsouza. The prototype took 3 business days against the existing telematics feed; a pilot with 40 drivers ran 2 days; the go/no-go conversation happened that same afternoon, since all three were already in the building. Total: 3 + 2 + 0 = 5 business days from concept to decision, with rollout to all 340 drivers beginning the next day. Divide 45 by 5: Ishan's loop ran roughly nine times faster — not because anyone was smarter, but because named approvers had dropped from five committees to three people in one room.

Now change one input. Suppose Ishan closes a Series C in early 2027 and hires a VP of product between Priya and Rohan, plus a formal Thursday review, because its insurance partners now require sign-off on safety claims. The prototype still takes 3 days, but waits for the next Thursday — up to 4 more days — and the insurer's check adds 5 more: roughly 12 to 14 days total. Ishan is still three to four times faster than Indraprastha ever was, but the gap has closed from ninefold to threefold in a single funding round — the mechanism behind the next topic this one unlocks.

Fig. 2 — The same feature, three organisational shapes.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Ambiguity is not the same as chaos. A startup with no decision-making structure at all is dysfunctional, not "high-ambiguity" in any useful sense. The PM's job is to add just enough structure that a decision can be made and remembered, not to import a five-committee process wholesale.

Regulatory intensity outranks company age. A twelve-month-old lending startup already needs Reserve Bank of India–grade documentation before it can touch a customer's money. "Young" does not mean "low alignment cost" once a product touches money, health data, or safety — as fatigue alerts eventually did once Ishan's insurer got involved.

Influence currency does not track title. A newly hired associate PM with the founder's direct trust can move faster than a senior PM who lacks it; the reverse mistake — assuming a senior bigco title substitutes for the relationships needed to get five sign-offs — is just as common.

What this model cannot tell you. Knowing where influence comes from does not say whether the startup will still have runway in fourteen months, or whether bigco politics will reward the "right" behaviour. Those are questions about survival and incentives, not about decision mechanics.

It is confused with scope of role. A PM can have wide scope and almost no real influence if every call needs five sign-offs, or narrow scope and total control. This topic explains the source of authority; the next explains its width.

Transitions fail in both directions, and size alone is a poor proxy for stage. Ex-bigco PMs who join startups over-invest in consensus-building, exactly as Rohan did on day nine, and stall; ex-startup PMs who join bigcos under-invest in alignment and get quietly overridden. An eighteen-month-old startup selling into enterprise customers may already need bigco-grade internal alignment, because its customers' procurement teams impose that structure from outside.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace, early stage and large company

The influence source described so far holds inside a single company, but it also shifts along a second axis: what kind of product the company sells. A consumer product at an early stage draws influence almost entirely from experiment velocity; the same product at bigco scale draws it increasingly from brand and legal gatekeeping, since one bad headline reaches millions overnight. A B2B startup sits in between from day one: its influence is partly borrowed from two or three design-partner customers whose contracts already impose structure. A marketplace concentrates influence in whoever can see both sides of the transaction — one PM often owns the whole liquidity loop early on — while a large marketplace splits that influence across category, fulfilment and trust-and-safety teams who must all agree before anything ships.

7. Common mistakes

Importing consensus-building into a startup. Symptom: a new PM's calendar fills with alignment meetings while nothing ships. Misunderstanding: treating alignment as the source of credibility, when credibility here comes from resolved ambiguity. Diagnostic: count prototypes shipped against meetings scheduled in the first thirty days — meetings outnumbering ships three to one means the wrong playbook.

Shipping without sign-off at a bigco. Symptom: a feature ships fast and gets pulled within a week over a compliance issue nobody flagged. Misunderstanding: assuming speed alone earns influence. Diagnostic: before launch, ask whether every named approver has actually seen the final version, not an earlier draft.

Mistaking alignment for outcomes at a bigco. Symptom: a PM with excellent stakeholder relationships and polished decks, but thin shipped results, whose promotion stalls for reasons that feel unfair. Misunderstanding: forgetting alignment is a means to shipping something that works, not a substitute for it. Diagnostic: can the PM name, with a number attached, what changed for a customer because of the last three things they aligned everyone on?

8. What good looks like

Two weeks later, Rohan tried something different with a second feature — an in-cab audio nudge to pair with the fatigue alert. Instead of scheduling six calendars, he walked to Priya's desk with a rough prototype already running on his phone and asked one question: "If this tests well with ten drivers on Monday, can I ship it to everyone by Thursday?" She said yes on the spot. He looped in Aman by message, not meeting, since Aman only needed to know the pilot drivers would be his own team. The pilot ran Monday and Tuesday; the decision took ten minutes; the feature reached all 340 drivers by Thursday morning, inside the runway Ishan actually had. Nothing about the idea itself was cleverer than the fatigue alert — what changed was that Rohan spent his time building evidence instead of consensus.

9. What Rohan decided, and what to carry forward

Rohan kept the six-person meeting for one thing only: a monthly update on what had shipped and why, so no one was surprised in front of Priya. Everything else he decided case by case, using the diagnostic he wished he had run on day one — who actually holds this decision right, and what evidence, not what agreement, will move them. He also began tracking which decisions had started needing more than three people, since that drift, he now understood, was the earliest signal that the company's stage was changing under him again.

The natural next question is how a PM renegotiates the scope of their own role as that drift continues, rather than absorbing it silently. Two questions worth sitting with: when your influence next stalls, is it because you have not resolved enough ambiguity, or because you have not built enough alignment — and how would you know which, before spending two weeks finding out the hard way?

Two Clocks: Yashodhan Digital and the Xipra Integration

Hyderabad, Sunday, 4 October 2026

1. The Night Before

The Gachibowli office was empty except for the security desk when Sujata Kaul came back at nine on Sunday evening to print the pre-read one more time. She had already sent it. She wanted to see it on paper, the way the board sub-committee would at eight-thirty the next morning, because on paper her recommendation occupied a single slide and looked far more settled than it was.

Sujata, forty-four, was President of Yashodhan Digital, the software and aftermarket-services division of Yashodhan Engineering Group, a Hyderabad-listed maker of pumps, compressors and process equipment with ₹41,200 crore of group revenue in FY2026. Nine months earlier the group had bought Xipra Plant Systems, a five-year-old Coimbatore company that had put maintenance workflows on the phones of shift technicians in textile mills, foundries and auto-ancillary plants across Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. The price was ₹640 crore up front and up to ₹140 crore more if Xipra's standalone recurring revenue reached ₹165 crore by 31 March 2027. The board approved it in eleven minutes.

The question on Monday's agenda was narrower and much harder: what the combined product organisation should look like from 1 January 2027. Sujata had three structures on the slide. She had begun the week certain of the first and ended it unable to defend any of them for four minutes at a stretch. What she kept returning to was not the boxes. It was that two groups of product managers in the same division, doing recognisably the same job, drew their ability to make anything happen from entirely different sources — and that she could not move one into the other's world without switching off the supply.

2. Yashodhan Engineering, and the Decision That Still Binds

The group was founded in 1971 as a pump workshop in Balanagar. By 2026 it sold process equipment to refineries, fertiliser plants, cement works and textile mills, and made a third of its profit on aftermarket spares and service. Yashodhan Digital had been carved out in 2019 on a sensible thesis: the group knew where forty thousand of its own machines were installed, so it should sell the software that watched them. By FY2026 the division was at ₹610 crore of revenue and 740 people.

The decision that constrained everything Sujata could now propose had been taken in 2021, before her time. A software-generated recommendation deferred an overhaul interval on a compressor train at a client's plant in Gujarat; the machine ran eleven days past its window and failed. Nobody was hurt, the claim settled at ₹9 crore, and the insurer's auditors spent four months in the division's offices. The group's response was the Gate process — five gates from concept to field release, with mandatory engineering sign-off from the equipment business on anything touching a maintenance interval, a torque value or a pressure limit. In 2022 the division also committed to a single group platform stack under a ₹210 crore enterprise agreement, partly so audit trails would live in one place. Rajat Mehrotra's organisation had been built to run that machinery, and had, without a repeat incident, for five years.

Xipra had been bought precisely because it did not work that way. Senthil Kalyanaraman started it in 2018 after a Tiruppur mill lost four days of production because the only man who knew which bearing to order had gone to his village. Its product shipped weekly, in Tamil and Kannada as well as English, and its biggest week of the year was the Ayudha Pooja shutdown, when customers' machines stopped, were garlanded, and were opened up. At acquisition Xipra served 2,400 plants with ₹118 crore of ARR and 190 employees.

3. The Industry

The market had three tiers and no settled shape. At the top were the global asset-performance suites — Siemens, SAP, ABB, Honeywell — sold to large process plants through integrators such as TCS or Infosys, at deal sizes starting around ₹15 crore. At the bottom were spreadsheets, WhatsApp groups and paper logbooks, still the default in mid-size manufacturing. The contested middle was where Xipra and its venture-funded rival Xamata Maintenance Cloud of Bengaluru had grown: plants with fifty to six hundred assets, an owner who signed cheques personally, and technicians whose first computer was a smartphone.

Policy had been kind to that middle. Production-linked incentive schemes pushed capital expenditure into electronics, auto components and speciality chemicals, and GST e-invoicing normalised digital records in firms that had resisted them. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had, less conveniently, made technician identity data — photographs, phone numbers, location traces from the app — something the group's legal team now reviewed line by line.

Exposure ran outward too. The division's largest contract, ₹31 crore a year, was with Yasira Industrial Holdings LLC of Dubai, covering 1,900 assets across the UAE and Oman, managed from Singapore by Corinne Tay. Yaqeen Reliability Systems of Gurugram had courted the same Gulf accounts for two years. In North America, where Vikram Bhalla sold from New Jersey, the parent's name opened doors no Coimbatore start-up could: buyers wanted a balance sheet and a master services agreement before a demo.

4. What Happened, and What Turned Out To Be Wrong

The integration had been designed as a gentle one. The signed plan gave Xipra twelve months of autonomy, a separate profit-and-loss statement and its own release train; shared services moved to the group immediately. Exhibit 1 shows the timeline as the integration office recorded it.

Three things believed in January were no longer believed in October. The first was that the Gate process could be applied selectively. In June, after a Xipra release changed a lubrication-interval default for compressors the group itself manufactured, the equipment business asked for Gate 3 to cover Xipra too, and nobody could argue against it on the merits. Median time from idea to production on Xipra's line went from nine days to twenty-six (Exhibit 2); the argument since is whether that is a cost or a price.

The second was that Xipra's revenue was separable. By September, much of the growth in Xipra's standalone ARR had been sourced by Yashodhan's own field sales force, who had found that a ₹6 lakh Xipra subscription closed in five weeks where a ₹4 crore platform deal took nine months. Finance and Xipra's commercial team could not agree how to attribute those deals, and ₹19 crore of ARR sat in dispute, astride the earn-out threshold (Exhibits 3 and 4).

The third was that the engineering platform would converge. In July, Faiz Qureshi's team in Bengaluru found two Xipra services — spares-catalogue search and the offline sync layer — running outside the approved stack, on infrastructure procured on a corporate card in 2024 and never migrated. Faiz marked it medium severity and had not escalated it, because migration would take a quarter of Xipra's engineering capacity inside the earn-out window.

11. Sunday, Eleven O'Clock

The printer finished. Sujata took the pages to the window. On the service road below, a lorry from the Balanagar works was turning towards the airport with a compressor skid strapped flat on its bed — the kind of machine the group had made since before she was born, the kind whose overhaul interval a product manager in Coimbatore could now change from a phone. Rajat had sent nothing, which was itself a position. She read the slide again, and the word she kept stopping on was not a number. It was "complete".

Where Influence Comes From: Shreya Kulkarni's Offer

Pune, Monday, 6 October 2025

1. The Decision

Shreya Kulkarni read the offer letter from Eklavya New Mobility for the fourth time that morning, in the second-floor conference room of Ehad Auto Exchange's Kharadi office in Pune. The subject line of Meenal Krishnan's covering email was polite but final: "Offer validity — response needed by Friday, 10 October." Four days. Outside the glass wall, the inspection bay was already busy — technicians walking scooters onto the diagnostic ramp Shreya had helped design eighteen months earlier, when Ehad had six hubs instead of forty-two. The offer was for Group Product Manager, pre-owned and EV resale, at Eklavya New Mobility, the new-ventures arm of Eklavya Mobility Ventures, one of India's largest diversified auto-to-mobility groups: ₹62 lakh fixed a year, nearly double her current ₹34 lakh, a pan-India charter on paper, and a logo her parents in Nashik would recognise. Her own founder, Devesh Rao, was two floors down, expecting an answer of his own by Friday on the counter-offer he had made her on Wednesday. Shreya had built her product instincts entirely inside Ehad; she had never worked anywhere large enough to have a "category head" or a "brand council," both of which appeared in Meenal's role description. She needed to decide not just which company paid better, but where, concretely, her influence as a product manager would actually come from in each place — and whether that changed what she should ask for before signing anything.

2. Company Background

Devesh Rao and a co-founder started Ehad Auto Exchange in Pune in 2019 on a simple wager: India's pre-owned two-wheeler market was large, informal and trust-starved, and company-run inspection hubs, backed by a 90-day warranty and financing tie-ups with lenders such as Bajaj Finserv and IDFC First Bank, could out-trust the local mechanic-broker who had run the market for decades. By late 2025, Ehad ran forty-two hubs across nine cities — Pune, Nashik, Nagpur, Indore, Aurangabad, Kolhapur and three in Bengaluru — moving roughly 9,800 vehicles a month at an annualised GMV near ₹340 crore. Its rivals were CredR, Cars24's two-wheeler vertical, OLX Autos and Droom, all chasing the same certified-resale promise with far deeper balance sheets. Ehad had closed a ₹85 crore Series B in early 2024, led by a Mumbai growth fund, and was fourteen months from a Series C that investors had told Devesh would hinge on proving the leadership bench could hold without him micromanaging every hub. Shreya had joined as the third product hire in 2022 and now owned the pricing-and-inspection engine — the algorithm setting a fair resale price from odometer reading, service history and 62 checkpoints, trusted enough that hub managers quoted it to a walk-in customer without a second approval.

3. The Situation

Meenal Krishnan, VP Product at Eklavya New Mobility in Chennai, had found Shreya through a conference talk on inspection algorithms in August. Eklavya Mobility Ventures — roughly ₹18,000 crore in group revenue across vehicle manufacturing, dealership finance and fleet leasing — had launched Eklavya New Mobility in 2024 to build a pan-India pre-owned and EV battery-swap network, using the parent's dealer footprint as an advantage against upstarts like Ehad. Meenal's pitch was expansive: Shreya would own product strategy for the entire resale line, across twenty-two states, with a team of eleven reporting through two senior PMs. What the pitch did not fully convey, Shreya learned from Kabir Anand, a Group Product Manager at the same division who had made an identical jump from a Gurugram logistics startup fourteen months earlier, was how a decision actually moved once it left a PM's desk. Kabir, on a call from Gurugram, was candid: a pricing change on his line had taken thirty-one days to ship in September, needing sign-off from the category head, the finance controller who owned resale-line margins, and the brand council protecting the parent's dealer relationships. "The scope on the org chart is real," Kabir said. "What you can decide alone by Friday is much smaller." Meanwhile in Pune, Devesh had made his own move: a promotion to VP Product, ₹40 lakh fixed, and a refreshed 0.4 percent ESOP grant, because Ehad's lead investor, watching the Series C runway, had flagged Shreya as a retention risk the board wanted resolved before December.

4. The People

Shreya Kulkarni — Senior Product Manager, Ehad Auto Exchange, Pune
Owns the pricing-and-inspection engine; must answer both offers by Friday, 10 October.
Devesh Rao — Co-founder & CEO, Ehad Auto Exchange, Pune
Wants Shreya to stay through the Series C raise; offered VP Product with a wider charter and fresh equity.
Meenal Krishnan — VP Product, Eklavya New Mobility, Chennai
Wants to close a strong hire before her division's Q3 headcount freeze; confident the charter will feel real once Shreya "earns the room's trust."
Kabir Anand — Group Product Manager, Eklavya New Mobility, Gurugram
Made the same startup-to-bigco move in 2024; wants Shreya to go in with open eyes about consensus, not to talk her out of joining.

5. Exhibits

The three exhibits together frame Shreya's real question. Exhibit 1 shows Eklavya's offer winning decisively on paper — title, pay, team size, geography — but Kabir's evidence behind the same table shows a wider charter and faster authority are not the same thing. Exhibit 2 shows why Devesh is fighting to keep her: Ehad is compounding fast, and product headcount has not kept pace with GMV, which is why one person's judgment still moves the whole pricing line. Exhibit 3 makes the mechanism visible — at Ehad, influence comes from proximity to the one person who can say yes; at Eklavya, it would have to come from something else, since no single yes exists.

6. The Options

Option A — Accept the Eklavya offer as written

Take the Group Product Manager role and the near-doubled pay, planning to earn real authority over year one by building credibility with the category head and finance. Upside: compensation, brand, a larger canvas if it works. Cost: Exhibit 3's cycle time is a real risk to year-one performance, and Kabir's experience suggests the "pan-India charter" will feel narrower than on paper.

Option B — Decline and stay at Ehad as VP Product

Accept Devesh's counter, keep the fast, founder-adjacent decision rights she already has, and bet on Ehad's trajectory through the Series C. Upside: proven influence, upside equity in a company she helped build, and a board that has just signalled she is core to its story. Cost: lower pay, a smaller brand name on her resume, and key-person exposure if growth stalls before the next round.

Option C — Counter-propose narrower, explicit authority at Eklavya

Tell Meenal she will join only if the offer letter names one sub-line — say, two-wheeler resale pricing, closest to her Ehad experience — where she holds sole sign-off up to a stated margin threshold, with category head, finance and brand council review reserved for exceptions above it. Upside: converts an ambiguous, wide charter into a smaller one with real teeth, borrowing Exhibit 3's logic rather than hoping to out-negotiate it after joining. Cost: a narrower title-in-practice than "pan-India," and a real chance Eklavya's structure cannot grant a written carve-out at all — in which case Shreya learns that before resigning from Ehad, not after.

7. Questions for Discussion

  1. At Ehad, what specifically gives Shreya influence over the pricing engine — title, data, or her relationship with Devesh? Would it survive a company three times Ehad's size?
  2. At Eklavya, Exhibit 1 lists a title, a headcount and a geography. Which, if any, is a source of influence rather than a description of scope?
  3. Kabir made the same move fourteen months ago and is candid, not discouraging. What does his account add that Meenal's pitch and Devesh's counter cannot tell Shreya alone?
  4. Of the three options, which treats "where influence comes from" as something to negotiate before signing, rather than something to discover afterward?

8. A Note for the Learner

This topic's lens is a simple distinction: at a startup, influence typically comes from proximity — to the founder, to the customer, to the one person who can say yes today — while ambiguity about the role's formal edges is the price of that speed. At a large company, influence typically comes from alignment — moving a proposal through the specific people who each hold a partial veto — while formal scope on an org chart can be wide even when actual freedom to decide is narrow. A well-reasoned answer engages both halves, not a simple pay-versus-purpose trade-off.

A defensible path is Option C. It does not romanticise the startup, since Exhibit 2 shows Ehad's dependence on one generalist's judgment is a fragility Devesh must fix regardless of Shreya's choice. Nor does it treat "pan-India charter" as more powerful than "owns pricing outright," since Exhibit 3 shows a wide charter without sign-off authority is only surface area. By asking Eklavya to name one sub-line with real, written decision rights, Shreya converts an open question — will I have influence there? — into a testable one before resigning from a role where she already knows the answer. If Eklavya cannot grant that carve-out, she has learned something decisive, at the cost of a few days' delay rather than a year of hers.

Product Operations

The system behind the team: what it costs, when it becomes the problem it was built to solve, and where practitioners still disagree.

1. Two decisions, one month apart

On 14 August 2026, Vikram Sundaram, Chief Product Officer of Tarkeeb Commerce Cloud, read a calendar audit he had commissioned reluctantly. Tarkeeb sells merchandising, store-operations and supply-planning software to retail chains in India and the Gulf; FY26 revenue was ₹1,240 crore across eleven product lines and 142 product managers. Its product operations group, two people in 2023, now numbered nineteen, and nobody disputed it had been necessary. The audit showed that median time from a validated problem to a first customer-visible release had risen from 9.4 weeks in Q1 FY25 to 16.8 in Q1 FY27, that artefacts required for a quarterly review had gone from four to eleven, and that the average PM spent 14.5 of a 40-hour week on things product ops owned. Vikram's question was not whether to have a system behind the team, but which parts to kill, and by what test he could defend that to those who built them.

Three weeks later, on 3 September, Nandita Phadke faced the opposite question in Pune. Quwwat Grid Systems makes commercial battery-storage hardware and sells alongside it an AI dispatch optimiser deciding when each site charges and discharges against tariff, load and grid signals. Revenue was ₹310 crore; there were 26 PMs, fourteen near firmware, twelve on dispatch. On 19 March a fortnightly retrain shipped and mis-scheduled discharge at forty industrial sites through the first monsoon week, costing demand-charge penalties Quwwat partly absorbed. The review found no bug: the evaluation corpus of 340 cases held no monsoon load shapes, and no one owned it. Nandita had budget for three people and had to decide whether product ops here meant roadmap and research hygiene, or custody of an evaluation set for a product whose behaviour changed without a code change.

 Tarkeeb Commerce CloudQuwwat Grid Systems
Product typeEnterprise software, 11 linesHardware plus AI-native

Exhibit 1 — one topic, reached from opposite ends of its life cycle.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Product operations is the deliberately maintained infrastructure — shared tooling, governed data definitions, research operations and recurring decision rituals — through which a product organisation converts individual competence into repeatable output. Two clauses do the work. Deliberately maintained: someone is accountable, so the scaffolding does not decay into whatever the last reorganisation left. Repeatable: the product is lower variance in decision quality, not a higher ceiling. Ops does not decide what to build; it decides how the deciding happens.

The lineage is older than the label. Taiichi Ohno's standardised work at Toyota established the proposition most product ops people inherit without reading: a standard is the baseline from which improvement is measured, and where there is no standard there can be no improvement. Shewhart and Deming added the statistical companion: reducing variation is a distinct objective from raising the average. Sales operations, from the 1990s, proved the organisational form — once performance depends on tooling, territory data and definitions, a specialist group owns them rather than the best rep. DevOps after 2009 and Google's site reliability engineering added the negotiated-budget idea, that reliability is traded rather than maximised. Team Topologies, published by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais in 2019, gave the shape now most used: an enabling team measured by other teams' throughput, not its own. The label hardened between 2018 and 2023, in practitioner writing from product-led firms such as Pendo and Amplitude, the ResearchOps community around Kate Towsey's work, and Melissa Perri and Denise Tilles's treatment.

Four positions compete, and good will does not reconcile them.

The functional school
Ops is a permanent discipline with its own ladder, budget and craft. Will sign: standards, data governance and research infrastructure are specialist work that degrades when done part-time. Will not sign: ops should own prioritisation or strategy.
The leadership-failure school
Associated with Marty Cagan's writing: in strong product companies this is the product leader's job, and a large ops function is a symptom of leaders who stopped doing it. Will sign: coaching and clear ownership boundaries remove most of the demand. Will not sign: that the demand is intrinsic to scale.
The platform school
Ops is an internal platform team whose users are PMs: adoption is the metric, mandates a failure signal. Will sign: a standard nobody would voluntarily adopt is a bad standard. Will not sign: compliance rates as evidence of value.
The federated school
Ops is a guild of rotating practising PMs with no permanent staff. Will sign: proximity to real work keeps standards honest. Will not sign: that a rotation cannot sustain a semantic layer or a panel — which is where it is weakest.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Experts do not begin with tools. They begin by counting interfaces, because interfaces generate the demand. With p pods sharing customers, data and release trains, the bilateral agreements needed to keep them consistent number p(p − 1)/2. At Tarkeeb's eleven lines that is 55 pairs; reconciling each costs about 1.5 hours a quarter, or 82.5 hours, and grows quadratically with every new line. A published standard replaces that with conformance: eleven pods each checking themselves against one definition. That is the economic case in one sentence — it converts an O(p²) coordination cost into an O(p) conformance cost plus a fixed maintenance cost.

Stated that way the trade has a break-even, and the break-even is per standard, not per function. Let N be the pod count, clocal the hours each pod spends doing the thing its own way including reconciliation, cconf the hours it spends conforming, and Cmaint the central hours to keep the standard alive.

Enforce centrally when N × (clocal − cconf) > Cmaint, then add the expected cost of the errors the standard prevents. Below that line the standard is a transfer of work from the centre to the teams.

Vikram ran all eleven of Tarkeeb's standards through this; six passed. Exhibit 2 shows five, per quarter, with N = 11. The pattern is instructive. Standards governing a shared artefact with one correct answer, such as a metric definition, an incident severity scale or a participant panel, clear the line easily, because local cost is dominated by reconciliation that vanishes entirely. Standards governing a pod's expression of its own thinking, such as a narrative memo template or a launch checklist, fail: conforming costs more than thinking freely and no reconciliation saving is recovered.

Exhibit 2 — hours per quarter. The roadmap row loses on hours and Vikram kept it anyway, because its value is a single answer to a question asked from outside, which the formula does not price.

Two second-order effects separate expert from competent practice. The first: ritual design controls decision latency through work in progress, not agenda quality. Tarkeeb's weekly product council carried 23 open decisions and closed about four a week; by Little's Law, latency is work in progress over throughput, or 5.75 weeks. The ops group's instinct was to improve the pre-read, which raised preparation cost per item and lowered throughput, lengthening the queue it meant to shorten. Delegating three classes of decision to pod leads cut work in progress to nine and latency to 2.25 weeks without touching the agenda.

The second: research operations is a marketplace in miniature and fails on the supply side first. Tarkeeb ran 310 customer conversations in the quarter; only 22 were later cited by a PM who had not run them, a reuse yield of 7.1 per cent. The same forty accounts absorbed most requests, and panel response rates had fallen from 61 to 38 per cent in a year. Raising reuse to 31 per cent — 96 studies, each saving roughly eleven hours of fieldwork — recovers about 814 hours a quarter, but only if tagging and synthesis are enforced at capture, the step almost always left implicit.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are testable. First: are there enough interfaces to make coordination quadratic? Tarkeeb, eleven lines sharing retail customers, emphatically yes; Quwwat, two surfaces and 26 PMs, nearly no — so Nandita cannot justify ops on coordination grounds. Second: does the same question recur with one correct answer? Yes for Tarkeeb's metric definitions; yes for Quwwat's eval corpus, asked fortnightly. Third: is the cost of inconsistency borne by someone who can see it? Tarkeeb's surfaces in board packs; Quwwat's as demand charges on forty customer bills. Fourth: will the standard survive without its sponsor? The test most often skipped.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. Before product-market fit, variance is the search mechanism, and reducing it destroys the thing the company is doing. Where the real defect is unclear ownership, ops absorbs the symptom and removes the pressure that would have forced a boundary decision — Tarkeeb's nineteen were partly a substitute for a platform team it never funded. And where judgement is the scarce input, standardising its expression degrades it.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

In multi-product companies the binding constraint is the customer identity key. Tarkeeb's roadmap tool, CRM, warehouse and support desk resolved "a customer" to four different keys, so every cross-line question needed a human join; no dictionary fixes that, and mature companies solve it in the data model, not the process. In two-sided businesses, supply and demand legitimately need different definitions and cadences; the workable pattern is separate local dictionaries plus a small governed set of shared network-health metrics. The failure is forcing one template across both, which sank the third example below.

In regulated products, ops carries the evidence chain. Qanaat Insurance Cloud, a Mumbai distribution platform selling to insurers under the IRDAI regime, ships about 520 tracked changes a year, each needing a traceable requirement-to-test-to-approval packet. Assembling one by hand took 6.5 hours; an ops-built generator reading the ticket system cut it to forty minutes, recovering roughly 2,770 hours a year and cutting external audit findings from fourteen to three. That is the clearest financial case for the function anywhere, and the one least often made.

Hardware plus software fails at cadence, not tooling. Quwwat's fourteen-week tooling lead time and weekly software train make a commitment in one system a different kind of promise in the other; mature firms keep two roadmaps and one coupling document listing only the dependencies that cross, not the single roadmap they describe in interviews. AI-native products move the artefact of record. When behaviour changes on a retrain with no code change, the PRD stops being the thing under governance and the evaluation set becomes it. Quwwat's corpus grew from 340 cases to 612, including 94 seasonal load shapes, gated at no more than two per cent regression on any of seven site archetypes across 26 retrains a year. Ops for that product is eval operations.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Ops reduces variance; it does not raise the ceiling

The tell is which statistic a leader quotes. Competent practitioners report median cycle time. Experts report the ninetieth percentile and the spread, because the function's product is the distance between the best pod and the worst. The obvious reading — that good ops makes everyone faster — is wrong: it slows the strongest pod slightly and lifts the weakest a lot, and a leader who does not say so will lose the argument with their best PM.

Every standard is a tax with a beneficiary

The tell is where the standard's author sits. When the people who wrote the launch checklist are the people who read launch reports, cost lands on pods and benefit at the centre, and adoption stays grudging however sound the content. Experts name payer and collector before publishing; where they differ, they either compensate the payer with tooling or drop the standard.

The artefact count ratchets up unless someone owns deletion

The tell is one question: what has this function retired in twelve months? At Tarkeeb the answer was nothing, which is how four artefacts became eleven without a single bad decision. Each addition was defensible; the aggregate took 36 per cent of PM capacity. Experts set an explicit deletion quota, because addition has a sponsor and deletion never does.

Enforcement lives in the data layer, not the document

The tell is pulling the same number from two dashboards. A definition in a wiki states intent; a definition compiled into a shared semantic layer both dashboards must query is a constraint. The obvious reading is that the dictionary was ignored. Usually it was read, agreed, and then quietly diverged, because nothing structural prevented it.

Rituals decay into reporting, and talk-time reveals it

The tell is the speaking-time ratio between the person who will decide and the people presenting. In a functioning review the decider talks a third of the time, asking. When presenters hold eighty per cent of the floor, the meeting is a status broadcast in a decision forum's clothes, and the fix is changing who prepares what, not extending the slot.

The ops-to-PM ratio diagnoses dysfunction, not maturity

The tell is what the ratio absorbs. Tarkeeb's one ops person per 7.5 PMs read internally as advanced practice; read against eleven lines with no platform team and no agreed ownership boundaries, it was a missing architecture paid for in coordination labour. Experts ask what would let the ratio fall; if the answer is an org-design change, the ops budget is financing avoidance.

Ops legitimacy is borrowed and expires

The tell is what happens when a standard is challenged. If the ops lead escalates to the sponsoring executive, the standard was never load-bearing; it was that executive's authority in a document. If the lead resolves it by showing the pod its own numbers, the standard has independent standing and outlives its sponsor. Most ops functions die in the quarter after their sponsor moves, and this is why.

For AI products, the governed artefact moves

The tell is who may add a case to the evaluation set, and whether anyone may remove one. Competent practitioners govern PRDs and release notes for a model-backed product and are surprised when behaviour drifts anyway. Experts treat the eval corpus as the specification of record, under the change control a schema would get, and write the gate as a per-segment regression threshold, not one aggregate score.

7. How it actually differs, and where it does not

Two pillars barely vary. Governed metric definitions and a functioning research repository earn their keep in consumer, B2B, enterprise, platform and hardware contexts alike, and claims of uniqueness here are usually avoidance. What genuinely differs is the release and decision machinery, set by cadence and by who bears the cost of an error.

B2B and enterpriseCommitment governance: win/loss, advisory boards, the PRD-to-contract seam

Hardware plus softwareTwo roadmaps, one coupling document; cadence, not tooling, is the problem

Exhibit 3 — differences worth designing for; what is omitted is broadly common.

Stage changes the answer more than type does. Before fit, the right amount of formal ops is close to none. From roughly fifteen to fifty PMs one generalist can hold the whole system. Past fifty the quadratic term bites and the function is cheaper than its absence. Past about 120, as at Tarkeeb, the risk inverts: the danger is a system that has outgrown the deletion discipline needed to keep it honest.

8. Three worked examples

Tarkeeb's de-scaling. At ₹4,100 an hour loaded, 14.5 ops-owned hours a week across 142 PMs and 48 working weeks is about 98,800 hours, or ₹40.5 crore a year — 36 per cent of a PM payroll of roughly ₹120 crore. Retiring the five standards that failed the break-even test and delegating three decision classes out of the weekly council was modelled to return 4.9 hours a week per PM, about ₹13.7 crore of capacity, while cutting ops from nineteen to twelve. Nothing retired was individually wasteful; the aggregate was.

Qanaat's compliance engine. The insurance platform's evidence generator is the cleanest positive case here because the counterfactual is observable: without it, 520 changes times 6.5 hours is 3,380 hours of pure transcription a year, and the audit findings it removed carried remediation cost besides. Ops paid for itself in one audit cycle. Note what made it work — the standard governed an artefact with exactly one correct form, imposed from outside.

Talaash Mobility Networks, and what failure looks like. Talaash, a Gurugram intercity freight marketplace, stood up a fourteen-person Product Excellence Office in early 2024 and mandated one PRD template, one discovery protocol and eleven review artefacts across both sides of its marketplace. Template compliance rose from 31 to 94 per cent in two quarters, reported as success. Experiments launched fell from 58 a quarter to 23, supply-side PM attrition rose from 11 to 34 per cent annualised, and median decision latency reached 5.1 weeks. The diagnosis: supply-side work — recruiting fleet owners — and demand-side work had been forced onto definitions fitting neither. The recovery cut the office from fourteen to five, kept three enforced standards (identity keys and metric definitions, an incident taxonomy, the participant panel), and republished the rest as an opt-in default kit. Experiments recovered to 47 a quarter; latency fell to 2.3 weeks; compliance settled at 68 per cent on three standards, the number the new lead reported.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Each is cheap to catch early and expensive after a sponsor change or an attrition spike, because by then the remedy looks like an attack on people rather than a standard.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should the function be permanent? The leadership-failure position is stronger than critics allow: several of the best-regarded product organisations of the last two decades ran with small or no ops groups, and most ops demand traces to leaders not setting definitions or boundaries. It would be wrong if coordination cost were quadratic beyond what leadership attention can scale to meet — which the Tarkeeb arithmetic suggests above some size. The functional position rests on specialist-craft evidence: semantic layers and panels degrade when nobody owns them full-time. It would be wrong if those artefacts proved maintainable by a rotation, which the federated school asserts and has not demonstrated at scale.

Who owns metric definitions? Product ops claims them because product decisions depend on them; data teams claim them because the semantic layer is theirs. Both are coherent and the split is unresolved; what is not defensible is Tarkeeb's arrangement, where product ops owned the words and nobody owned the query.

Mandate or default? The platform school's adoption-over-compliance rule has a real limit: some standards, notably regulatory evidence and identity keys, must be universal to work at all, and 68 per cent voluntary adoption is failure, not signal. The honest resolution is that standards divide into the few that must be mandated and the many that must earn use — and that most functions misclassify.

Does ops improve outcomes at all? The field's open question, and it should be stated plainly. Every measured improvement above is a process metric: cycle time, reuse yield, audit findings, latency. The causal link from those to revenue or retention rests on argument, not controlled evidence, because no company runs the counterfactual. A practitioner who claims otherwise overstates what is known.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied product ops proposes a function, a tool stack and templates. Someone who has internalised it counts interfaces first, then treats each standard as a separate investment with its own break-even and named payer. They design rituals by managing work in progress rather than agendas, build enforcement into the data layer and leave expression to the teams. They hold a deletion quota as seriously as a delivery target, watch what their strongest PM routes around, and say out loud that the product is lower variance, not higher performance, which is why they know when to shrink it.

12. What each of them decided

Vikram cut Tarkeeb's ops group from nineteen to twelve, retired five of eleven standards on the break-even test, and kept the roadmap system of record despite its negative arithmetic, on the ground that it answers a question from outside the organisation. He moved metric definitions into a joint charter with the data platform team, so the words and the query had one owner, and gave the ops lead a standing quota: one standard retired each quarter, reported alongside anything added. At 142 PMs, he argued, the risk had inverted and the function needed a brake more than an accelerator.

Nandita hired three at Quwwat, none for roadmap hygiene, which 26 PMs did not need. One took custody of the evaluation corpus with change control and the per-segment release gate; one took the definitions spanning hardware telemetry and software analytics, where one site appeared under two identifiers; one took the coupling document between the fourteen-week hardware train and the weekly software train. She declined to standardise PRDs: with twelve senior PMs on dispatch, judgement was her scarce input and formatting would not improve it.

  1. Tarkeeb's roadmap standard fails the break-even test and Vikram kept it. Defensible exception, or the start of the ratchet he is trying to stop — and what evidence distinguishes the two?
  2. Talaash's office reported compliance monthly and throughput never. Was the failure one of measurement, of mandate, or of forcing one template across a two-sided business — and which would you have caught first?
  3. If the causal link from product ops to business outcomes is unestablished, on what basis should a board approve a nineteen-person function — and would you approve Nandita's three?

13. Going deeper

Product org models sets the interface count this topic prices; the model is the upstream decision. Team topologies and ownership boundaries explains when a rising ops ratio is really a missing platform team — the diagnosis Tarkeeb got wrong for three years. The product management tool stack makes the data-model argument concrete: which tools can join on one customer key. Discovery at organisational scale is where research ops stops being a repository and becomes a question-allocation problem. Product reviews and decision forums supplies the work-in-progress arithmetic behind latency, and cross-functional rituals the mechanics of who prepares what. Managing product managers, hiring PMs and PM levels and career ladders matter next because every break-even depends on variance in the population governed — and hiring moves that variance faster than any standard can.

Waani Streaming Systems: Building the System Behind the Team

ISB Product Management Series · India · Six weeks to launch

1. A Saturday in Bengaluru

On the morning of 12 September 2026, Aparna Iyer sat in an empty conference room at Waani Streaming Systems' Indiranagar office, re-reading the incident report from three months earlier. In fifty-seven days, on the eve of Diwali, Waani planned to switch on its service in three new languages — Malayalam, Odia and Assamese — taking its catalogue to nine Indian languages and, the growth deck promised the board, another 9 million monthly viewers. Aparna, Waani's Head of Product, had until the end of the month to tell the board how the company would run this launch without repeating what had happened during the June cricket season. The honest answer, as of that Saturday, was that she did not know. What she did know was that the company's product teams no longer shared a single version of the truth, and that this was now a decision about the system behind the team, not about any one feature.

2. A company built on regional bandwidth

Waani was founded in Pune in 2019 by three engineers who had watched Hotstar and MX Player fight over English and Hindi metros while Tier-2 and Tier-3 India stayed underserved in its own languages. Waani's wager was narrow and deliberate: license regional film and television libraries, dub and subtitle them with AI-assisted localisation, and stream them reliably on 2G-adjacent networks in towns like Bhagalpur, Nellore and Rourkela. It worked. By 2026 Waani carried content in six languages, had struck data-bundling deals with Airtel and Jio, and served 42 million monthly active users on an annualised revenue run-rate of roughly ₹96 crore, split between subscriptions and advertising. A carrier-billing partnership with a Gulf telecom carried Waani into Non-Resident Indian households across the UAE, a small but high-margin slice of revenue that the sales team in New Jersey, led by Kevin Fernandes, had built into the next funding pitch. Waani's competitors were larger and better funded — Reliance's JioCinema, Times Internet's MX Player, Aha in Telugu, Hoichoi in Bengali — but none matched Waani's claim to being fastest and cheapest to stream in a small town. That claim depended entirely on operational discipline that, in September 2026, was fraying.

3. What the June incident exposed

On 6 June, during a high-traffic India–Pakistan T20 simulcast, Waani's stream buffered badly for viewers on 3G and bundled-data connections outside metro India. The company's growth dashboard, built independently by the marketing analytics team, reported an 8 percent buffering rate and called the event a minor blip. Engineering's Grafana panels, built by a different team on different event definitions, showed 20 percent. A third number, assembled two weeks later by data scientist Devansh Oberoi from raw CDN logs because neither dashboard could be reconciled, put the true figure near 27 percent in Tier-3 towns specifically — the exact audience Waani existed to serve. The post-mortem's harder finding was organisational: no one owned the on-call rotation that night. The Pune engineering squad assumed Bengaluru had it; Bengaluru assumed a rotation that had quietly lapsed a month earlier still stood. Support tickets, meanwhile, had climbed steadily — from roughly 4,100 a month in April to 7,600 in August — and a growing share of them, Waani's customer-success lead Farah Hassan noted from Singapore, were being answered differently by different regional support desks because there was no shared source of truth for known issues. Each squad had its own dashboard, its own event taxonomy, and its own idea of what "resolved" meant. Waani had scaled its product surface faster than it had scaled the system that kept teams pointed at the same facts.

Exhibit 1 — The 6 June buffering incident: three teams, three numbers

No dashboard was wrong on its own terms; none used the same definition of a buffering event, and no one owned reconciling them until after the fact.

4. The people around the table

Aparna IyerHead of Product, BengaluruMust recommend a product-operations model to the board by 30 September, before the Diwali launch window closes.
Rakesh BhandariVP Engineering, PuneWants his 34 engineers shipping the language launch, not absorbed into new process; worries a product-ops hire becomes another approval layer.

Devansh OberoiData Scientist, TorontoRefuses to sign off on launch metrics until there is one agreed event taxonomy; currently spends a third of his week reconciling dashboards by hand.

Farah Hassan in Singapore and Kevin Fernandes in New Jersey were not in the room but shaped the deadline: Farah's regional support desks needed a shared playbook before nine languages went live at once, and Kevin's Gulf carrier partner had asked, pointedly, why Waani could not yet report a single, trusted uptime number for its board deck.

5. What it would cost to fix

Aparna asked her chief of staff to cost three paths against the same fifty-seven-day clock. The numbers, shown in Exhibit 2, made the trade-off concrete rather than philosophical.

Exhibit 2 — Three paths, costed against the 8-November launch

The timeline in Exhibit 3 shows why the calendar, not the budget, was the binding constraint: the fifty-seven days included a two-week code freeze before Diwali, leaving effectively six working weeks to design, build and rehearse whatever system Aparna chose.

Exhibit 3 — Of fifty-seven days, only about six working weeks fall before the pre-launch code freeze.

6. Aparna's options

Option A — Hire a permanent Head of Product Operations now. This builds the durable function Waani will eventually need: one owner for tooling, data access and rituals across every squad, in every language. Its cost is time — a credible search, in a market where good product-ops candidates are scarce, would likely miss the launch entirely, leaving the September problem unsolved when it matters most.

Option B — Appoint an internal interim owner and ship the minimum system. Aparna names a senior PM as interim product-ops lead for eight weeks: one shared incident dashboard, one on-call rota spanning Pune and Bengaluru, one weekly cross-team ritual before launch. It is fast and cheap, but it borrows bandwidth from an already-stretched PM and risks becoming permanent by default, without ever being properly resourced.

Option C — Bring in a product-ops consultancy for a fixed engagement. A contracted team stands up the tooling and playbooks against a clear brief, then hands off documentation. It arrives with less institutional memory of Waani's specific failure modes, and Rakesh worried openly that consultants who leave in December take the discipline with them.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, failed on 6 June — was it a tooling gap, a staffing gap, or a ritual gap? Does the answer change which option is right?
  2. Whose incentives does each option serve well, and whose does it strain — consider Rakesh's engineers, Lukas's research practice and Devansh's data trust?
  3. Given Exhibit 3's calendar, is "ready before launch" the right test for a decision that also has to hold after Diwali?
  4. Could Aparna combine elements of two options without doubling the cost or the confusion?

8. A note for the learner

Product operations is easy to underrate precisely because it produces no feature of its own. It is the system behind the team: the shared event taxonomy that lets Devansh trust a number the first time, the on-call rota that means someone always owns 2 a.m. in Pune, the single research repository that lets Lukas reuse what a viewer in Rourkela already told Waani. When that system is missing, every other function pays a hidden tax — reconciling dashboards, re-answering the same support ticket three ways, re-litigating whose number was right in June.

The case is built so that Option A is correct in principle and wrong for this clock: fifty-seven days do not permit a proper hire and a proper ramp. Option C outsources the very institutional judgment — which rituals fit Waani's specific culture and failure modes — that a consultancy is least equipped to build durably. The defensible path is Option B, run deliberately rather than as an afterthought: name an interim owner now, ship the minimum viable system — one dashboard, one rota, one weekly ritual — in time for the launch, and open the search for a permanent Head of Product Operations in parallel, so the interim arrangement has an explicit expiry date rather than becoming Waani's permanent, under-resourced answer to a problem it has now named twice.

Pakwan Restaurant Cloud: The System Behind Eleven Squads

For class discussion. Fictional: Pakwan Restaurant Cloud, Rangat Foods & Beverages, Pardaaz Retail Systems, Rutba Hospitality Group, Rivaaj Operating Partners, Paimaish Data Systems. Other firms named are real.

1. Sunday night, Gachibowli

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 27 September 2026, Ishani Kamat was still at her dining table in Kondapur with three versions of the same slide open. Each carried the title FY27 Product Operating Plan, and each answered differently the question the board would put to her in twelve hours: what was Pakwan Restaurant Cloud paying for when it paid for product operations, and was it working?

Ishani had been Vice-President of Product for two years and four months. The board met at ten on Monday at the Financial District office, one investor dialling in from Singapore and another from Mumbai; her agenda item was twenty-five minutes. Headcount had been frozen company-wide on 4 September. Rutba Hospitality Group, Pakwan's largest single customer, had a contractual exit window that opened on 15 November and had, in August, written a letter that a lawyer would call temperate and that everyone at Pakwan had read as a warning. And Zoya Qureshi, the Director of Product Operations whom Ishani had personally recruited twenty months earlier, had asked for thirty minutes on Tuesday — a meeting Ishani suspected was a resignation waiting for an outcome.

The three slides said, in order: expand product operations and give it release authority; dissolve it into the eleven squads; or hand the function to Rivaaj Operating Partners for nine months and ₹1.15 crore. What unsettled her was a fourth possibility she had not put on a slide: that all three answered a question Pakwan had never actually asked itself, and that what made product work here so expensive had been agreed in a sales meeting in 2023, long before anyone at the company said “product ops” out loud.

2. The company, and the promise it made in 2023

Pakwan Restaurant Cloud was founded in Hyderabad in 2018 by Tarun Sabharwal, an enterprise-software salesman, and Sukanya Raghavan, an engineer who had built payment switches. Their observation was ordinary and correct: India's restaurant sector was formalising fast under GST, delivery aggregation and landlords who wanted audited numbers, yet the software running a 40-outlet chain in Coimbatore was a billing counter bolted to a spreadsheet. Pakwan sold one platform — point of sale, kitchen display, inventory and recipe costing, menu sync to Swiggy and Zomato, GST e-invoicing, later an ONDC seller integration — to chains too large for a billing counter and too small to interest global vendors.

By September 2026 Pakwan served roughly 4,900 brands and 31,000 outlets on recurring revenue of about ₹168 crore, growing 34 per cent. Of 610 staff, 190 were engineers and 23 product managers across eleven squads. The Gulf supplied 14 per cent of revenue, where Rutba Hospitality Group alone ran 210 outlets in the UAE and Saudi Arabia; North America supplied nine, sold out of Edison, New Jersey into diaspora restaurant groups and, increasingly, mid-market American chains.

The decision that shaped everything after it was made in the second quarter of FY24. Pardaaz Retail Systems, a better-capitalised Gurugram competitor, had begun winning enterprise deals with a thinner, more opinionated product. Pakwan's answer, championed by Tarun and encoded in the sales deck as Tenant Freedom, promised every enterprise customer configurable workflows: its own approval chains, reconciliation rules and menu-publishing logic. It won deals. It also produced, by mid-2026, more than 1,400 live configuration flags, of which an audit could not explain about 300. Every squad now shipped into a surface that behaved differently for the forty largest customers, no two instrumented alike.

3. The industry around it

Indian restaurant technology in 2026 was a market of thin margins and thick integrations. Swiggy and Zomato set the tempo of a chain's week; a menu that failed to sync before a Friday promotion cost real money within the hour. ONDC had opened a second, lower-margin channel most chains wanted a presence on and none wanted to work by hand. Over it all sat regulation with teeth: falling GST e-invoicing thresholds, FSSAI traceability, and, from 2025, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, which turned every stored customer phone number into an obligation.

Pardaaz Retail Systems, the Gurugram competitor, shipped fewer features and shipped them the same way for everyone, so its release notes were short and its support desk knew what was in production. Pakwan's position — deep Indian compliance, hard aggregator integration, willingness to bend to the customer — was genuinely differentiated and genuinely expensive to hold.

The Gulf complicated matters. Rutba Hospitality Group's three-year contract, signed in March 2025 and worth about ₹18 crore, carried commitments Pakwan had never made before: 99.9 per cent availability on the ordering path, data residency for UAE customer records, and — a clause Ishani now read weekly — a monthly operations report giving “a single, reconciled account of incidents, root causes and remediation”. Pakwan had signed believing the clause described a document. It described a capability the company did not have.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Product operations at Pakwan began as a fix for one embarrassment. In November 2024 two squads shipped conflicting changes to the same tax-rate service nine days apart, and it took eleven days to establish which change had made which customer's invoices wrong. Ishani proposed a small central function, and in January 2025 Zoya Qureshi joined from a Mumbai fintech as Director of Product Operations with a one-sentence mandate: make it possible for eleven squads to work from the same facts.

Zoya's first year was, by the measures the company chose, a success. She consolidated roadmap tracking, stood up the research repository Lena Brandt in Berlin had demanded since 2023, published a shared event taxonomy, and instituted a Thursday operating review where every squad presented against the same six metrics. In April 2025 she rebuilt the cycle-time measure to draw from the work-tracking system rather than from PMs typing dates into a sheet. Median cycle time, 34 days before her arrival, was reported at 19 by FY26 Q4 — a number that reached two board decks and an investor update.

It was, Nikhil Rasquinha established in August 2026, not comparable. The old measure started the clock at ticket creation; the new one started it at sprint commitment. His reconstruction, in Exhibit 2, put the real improvement at about six days rather than fifteen. Nobody had concealed anything: the footnote existed, in an appendix, in one deck, in six-point type.

Meanwhile the incidents had not stopped. In February 2026 two squads implemented the same GST e-invoicing rounding change differently, each having inherited a different enterprise configuration profile, and 61 customers received a fortnight of invoices that had to be reissued. On the weekend of 18–19 July, during a heavily promoted aggregator campaign, a menu-synchronisation release pushed an incorrect item-availability flag to Rangat Foods & Beverages, a 140-outlet chain in Bengaluru. For eleven hours about a third of Rangat's menu showed as unavailable on delivery platforms. Credits came to ₹47 lakh, and Tarun now handled the January renewal personally.

The July post-mortem is where the company's account of itself split in two. Zoya's register blamed configuration sprawl: the release was tested against a standard tenant profile, and Rangat's was not. Abhijit Sule, Director of Engineering in Bengaluru, blamed release process: the change had skipped a canary stage his own team had defined but nobody enforced across squads. Both described the same hours; both were, on their own evidence, correct. When Ishani asked how many severity-1 and severity-2 incidents FY26 had contained, she received two answers — 38 from product operations, 61 from engineering's paging system — never reconciled, because reconciling them was exactly the work nobody had been given time to do.

8. The options as Ishani sees them

Option A — expand, and give the function authority. Product operations absorbs release management, owns one incident register, one severity definition and one metric dictionary, and certifies what ships. Zoya's argument: a function accountable for coherence without authority over releases is designed to fail. The objection is political — it breaks the freeze and gives six people a veto over 190 engineers whose director does not believe in it.

Option B — dissolve, and embed. The six move into squads under engineering managers. Abhijit's case: the work is real but the centralisation is not, because the people who know a squad's failure modes sit in it. The unanswered question is who then owns what exists only between squads — the taxonomy, the Rutba report, the reconciliation of Exhibit 3. In FY25, when that work belonged to everyone, one bad tax change took eleven days to find.

Option C — contract it out to Rivaaj. Nine months, ₹1.15 crore, defined scope: one incident register, an automated Rutba report, a configuration audit, playbooks. Meghna likes it because it is terminable. Its weakness is what no statement of work can hold — judgement about which rituals suit a company that sells Tenant Freedom, the judgement that leaves in June.

Option D — hold and trim. Keep the function, cut two roles, revisit after the Rutba window closes. The only option that requires no argument to be won this month, and the only one that guarantees the same conversation in March.

All four options changed who did the work and none changed how much work there was. The 1,410 flags would still be there on Tuesday; so would Gary's compensation plan and the promise it was built to sell. In her notebook Ishani had written one line, and nothing after it: is this an operating-model decision, or a product decision I am refusing to make?

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board expects a recommendation, not options. Headcount is frozen until the FY27 plan is approved, so any option that adds people requires Meghna to reopen the freeze publicly. Rutba's exit window opens on 15 November, and Shirin's view is that the relationship survives on the next two monthly reports. The Rangat renewal falls in January. The Paimaish licence runs to March 2028 regardless. DPDP remediation — consent records, retention windows, deletion on request across 31,000 outlets — is committed for the March quarter, unstaffed, and sits unfunded on Zoya's plan. Rivaaj's proposal expires on 10 October. Zoya's invitation for Tuesday, titled “30 mins”, remains unaccepted.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What problem was product operations created to solve in January 2025, and is that still the problem Pakwan has in September 2026?
  2. Exhibits 2 to 5 each come from someone with a stake in the outcome. Which would you show the board, and what would you say about those you leave out?
  3. Exhibit 3 shows two incident counts never reconciled. Under each of Options A to D, who would reconcile them — and what does that reveal about what the options actually differ on?
  4. Abhijit and Zoya describe the July incident accurately and reach opposite conclusions. What would make one of them more right, and what evidence would settle it?
  5. If Tenant Freedom is the source of the cost, what would revisiting it take, and who has the standing and the incentive to raise it before the Series D?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Ishani do first, what does she tell the board in twenty-five minutes, and what does she say to Zoya on Tuesday?

It was past one when Ishani closed the laptop without choosing a slide. She had written the three sentences she could defend before the board: that Pakwan's incidents were not random, that nobody could yet say how many there had been, and that neither fact was the fault of the six people whose jobs were on Monday's agenda. She could not decide whether saying so aloud would sound like clarity or like a general who had lost track of his own army. Outside, the Gachibowli traffic had thinned to the occasional delivery rider. Somewhere in the Rangat kitchens the Monday menu was being loaded by hand, because the head office had stopped trusting the sync.

Product Operations

1. A board pack with no single answer

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Ananya Kapoor, VP of Product at Faisla Payments Cloud, sat down to prepare the board pack and realised she could not answer a question she had been asked before: what does the roadmap actually say is shipping this quarter. Faisla, a Bengaluru-based provider of payment-acceptance and lending-as-a-service infrastructure to mid-market Indian retailers and NBFCs, had grown its product team from fourteen to fifty-eight people in eighteen months, across three lines — Payments, Lending-as-a-Service, and a newer Compliance Suite built for the tightening RBI reporting regime. Each line had its own roadmap tool, PRD template, and idea of what "committed" meant. In June, a board member had asked why a promised reconciliation feature had slipped twice; three leads gave three explanations, none matching what customer success had told the client.

The deeper problem surfaced when Ananya asked for every interview Faisla had run with lending customers in six months. Nobody knew, because "the research repository" was a Slack channel used inconsistently, and three customers had been interviewed separately by two pods the same week, asking overlapping questions. Commitments were missing their quarter by roughly forty percent, and the Series D lead investor had flagged "operational maturity" as an open risk. Ananya's task was to decide whether Faisla needed a formal system behind the team, and what it should contain.
