2. The idea

Product operations, usually shortened to product ops, is the set of shared tools, data access, research infrastructure, and recurring rituals that lets a product organisation make good decisions repeatably as it grows, instead of depending on individual PMs remembering, by hand, how things are done. It does not decide what to build. It maintains the scaffolding that makes many PMs, working on many things at once, behave like one coherent organisation.

The term entered common use between roughly 2018 and 2021, borrowed from the pattern sales operations had set for sales teams and DevOps for engineering: once a function outgrows what its best performers carry by instinct, someone has to own the infrastructure that lets everyone else approach that level. Melissa Perri and other practitioners writing then, alongside product-led companies such as Amplitude and Pendo whose growth forced the question, gave the role its name: metrics definitions, research operations, tooling administration, and onboarding new PMs. Before that, the work existed but was invisible, absorbed by whichever VP had the patience for it, and its cost showed up as duplicated research and roadmaps nobody trusted.

The sentence Ananya could repeat in a board meeting without sounding glib: product ops is what makes the fifty-eighth product manager's first launch look as disciplined as the fourteenth product manager's fiftieth, without either having to remember it unaided.

3. How it actually works

Building product ops is an assembly of four pillars practitioners usually blur together but which need separate decisions. The first is tooling: which roadmap tool is the single source of truth, which PRD template every pod uses, and what instrumentation standard every feature must meet before shipping. The second is data access: does every PM have self-serve access to true revenue and usage data, and who owns the definitions — what exactly counts as an "active merchant" — so two dashboards never quietly disagree. The third is research operations: a shared, tagged repository of every customer conversation, one recruiting panel so pods stop calling the same customers, and a synthesis format so insight survives the meeting it was shared in. The fourth is rituals: events — a roadmap review, a launch checklist, a blameless postmortem — that force the tools and data to actually get used.

The step most often skipped is sequencing. The instinct is to buy tools first, since they are procurable in a week, but tools without agreed rituals just add more places for inconsistency to hide. A more durable sequence starts with an audit — a small team spends two or three weeks mapping what exists, pod by pod — and from it comes a minimum viable system: one dictionary, one repository, one roadmap tool, piloted with a single willing pod. Its friction gets fixed before pod two, and only then does it fold into onboarding, which is what makes it durable rather than a cleanup that decays within a year.

4. A worked example: what duplication actually costs

Ananya wanted a number before asking the board to fund a two-person product ops team. A Faisla PM's loaded cost is roughly ₹28 lakh a year, or about ₹1,349 an hour across a 173-hour month. Pod leads estimated each of the fifty-eight PMs lost about six hours a month to work a shared repository and panel would make unnecessary — re-scheduling interviews another pod had already run, or re-deriving a metric someone had already agreed.

That is 58 × 6 = 348 duplicated hours a month, worth about ₹56.3 lakh a year in pure waste, not total research cost. Cutting that by roughly two-thirds, a figure the pilot pod supported, recovers about 226 hours a month, worth ₹36.6 lakh a year: short of the ₹50 lakh a two-person team would cost. Read alone, the investment looks marginal.

The second pass explains why timing matters. Faisla planned to grow from fifty-eight to about ninety PMs within a year. Unfixed at ninety, waste rises to ₹87.4 lakh a year. Built early, the same recovery rate applies to the bigger base, recovering about ₹56.8 lakh — clearly above the team's cost, and rising with every PM hired after. The lesson: fitting the system onto fifty-eight PMs is cheaper than retrofitting it onto ninety confused ones.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

It is infrastructure, not a junior PM's admin work

The common misread is handing the title to a junior hire doing scheduling and status-chasing. Real product ops owns definitions other people rely on; treating it as a dumping ground for logistics is the fastest way to make it fail.

It is not program or delivery management

Program managers track whether committed work ships on time. Product ops builds the infrastructure behind what gets committed to. A company can track delivery beautifully and still have no shared idea of what "good" looks like in a PRD.

It does not create insight or set strategy

Product ops cannot tell Ananya which of three roadmap bets is right. It guarantees whoever decides has clean data and a searchable history of what customers said; the judgement stays the leader's, and blaming the ops team when a bet fails mistakes infrastructure for judgement.

Below a certain size, formalising it is premature

Below roughly fifteen to twenty PMs, a strong VP, a shared drive, and a weekly sync usually do the job at lower cost. The formal function earns its keep once the VP can no longer hold the system in their own head.

It is not the same as company-wide "operations"

A COO's operations runs the whole business; product ops is scoped to how product decisions get made. Conflating the two staffs it against the wrong mandate.

Tools bought before rituals are agreed create sprawl

An analytics tool, a roadmapping tool, and a repository bought in one quarter without an enforcing ritual add three more places the truth might hide, not one place it reliably is.

It cannot diagnose whether the agreed metrics are right

An enforced dictionary guarantees everyone reads "active merchant" alike. It says nothing about whether that should matter versus loan quality — a judgement a newcomer should ask who last reviewed.

6. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products, with daily or weekly cadence, product ops leans toward experimentation infrastructure: guardrails on what an A/B test can ship without review, an always-on panel, and growth dictionaries every squad reads alike. In B2B products like Faisla's, cadence is slower and stakes higher, so it leans toward structured discovery — advisory boards, win/loss programmes, PRD discipline coupled to sales handoffs. In marketplaces, supply and demand sides often need separate dictionaries while sharing network-health metrics; the job there is coordination as much as tooling.

Stage matters as much as type. Pre-product-market-fit, heavy product ops is close to an anti-pattern: the team coordinates by conversation, and formal rituals mostly slow the search for fit. Past roughly fifty people, as Faisla had, the absence of the function starts costing real money. In a large, late-stage company, product ops usually becomes its own career ladder, owning new-PM onboarding and often the tool budget.

7. Common mistakes

The first is building a repository and assuming behaviour follows: PMs still schedule interviews from scratch months after launch, since a tool changes habits only when a ritual enforces it; the diagnostic is usage logs, not asking pods if they use it. The second is tool sprawl disguised as progress: three pods each buy a different roadmap tool, mistaking purchase for system; the diagnostic is one blunt question — if the CEO asked for the roadmap right now, how many places would someone look. The third is process for its own sake: velocity drops the quarter an ops team forms, since more approval gates gets confused with more discipline; the diagnostic is counting steps from idea to shipped experiment against six months ago. The fourth is a dictionary that isn't enforced: "active merchant" means different things on two dashboards, since a document was mistaken for a fix at the data layer; the diagnostic is pulling the same metric from both and comparing.

8. What good looks like

Ananya found her benchmark inside Faisla itself. The Compliance Suite pod, newest and smallest at nine PMs, had quietly built a lighter version of everything the company lacked: a shared document of every RBI requirement validated with a customer, tagged by which bank had confirmed it; a fifteen-minute Monday ritual against one dashboard, not three; and a self-imposed rule that no PM called a customer without checking whether someone else had asked that question recently. None of it was mandated — the pod's lead, hired from a company with mature product ops, had simply rebuilt habits she trusted. The result showed in the numbers: commitments missed by twelve percent that quarter against forty percent company-wide, with roughly half the PRD-to-first-test cycle time. Good product ops did not look dramatic. It looked like a fifteen-minute meeting nobody dreaded and a dashboard nobody argued with.

9. What Ananya decided

Ananya did not ask the board for a large function. She asked for two people, reporting to her, tasked first with a three-week audit across all three pods, then a minimum viable system built on the Compliance Suite pod's habits: one metrics dictionary, one shared repository with a single recruiting panel, and one roadmap tool as sole source of truth, piloted in the Lending-as-a-Service pod — the one under the most investor scrutiny, and so the most incentive to make it work. She deferred an instrumentation-standards tool until the first three rituals had survived a full quarter, resisting the sprawl the nuances had warned her about. The arithmetic said the system barely paid for itself at fifty-eight people but clearly would at ninety, where Faisla was headed; building it now was cheaper than retrofitting it later.

What she resolved to learn next was the product management tool stack, since tooling was the pillar she understood least, and discovery at organisational scale, since a repository alone does not guarantee fifty-eight PMs ask the right questions rather than merely different ones. Two questions worth sitting with: if your roadmap were pulled up right now, would everyone in the room recognise it as the same document; and when did anyone last check whether the metric your team optimises for still matters, rather than being simply the one everyone has agreed to stop arguing about.
